## Section-by-Section Notes

### Abstract & Introduction

- The core positioning — “first weakly-supervised LTA model trained exclusively with video transcripts” — is strong but, given the ambiguities around ATBA and CRF supervision, not fully justified. The paper should explicitly and rigorously define what “transcript-only” means (e.g., no timestamps, no partial boundaries, no next-action labels) and then prove that every component adheres to that constraint.
- The motivation for using transcripts as high-level structure is sound and well connected to prior weakly supervised TAS work. The relation to Kim et al. (2024) (language-only anticipators) is mentioned but not contrasted: in particular, those models also avoid frame-level labels but operate in a different regime. The paper could be more precise about what is distinct in the dense framewise setting.

### Related Work

- Coverage of weakly supervised TAS and dense LTA is adequate.  
- The description of Mate & Dimiccoli (2024) (TCCA) and the CRF component is slightly misleading: here they present their own CRF as a “stochastic variant”, but there is no explicit modeling of multiple futures in the CRF itself; the stochasticity arises from the sampling protocol. This is more a conceptual stretch than a technical flaw, but it does blur the relationship to prior CRF-based LTA.

### Methodology

**Problem Definition (Sec. 3)**

- The formalization mixes segment-level and frame-level viewpoints without fully disambiguating them. \(Y\) is a list of action segments, but later \(Y^{\hat{LTA}}\) and D are defined in a way that is closer to segment-level anticipation. Then almost all losses (Latba, CTC, CRF) are written in framewise terms.
- The assumption that D sums to 1 is inherited from early LTA works, but no explicit link is given between this normalized duration vector and the fixed-horizon βT used in the evaluation protocol. This makes the duration formulation feel somewhat decoupled from actual practice.

**Model Architecture (Sec. 3.1)**

- The use of class tokens E concatenated to video frames is an interesting design; however, it is not made clear how many queries or class tokens are present relative to the vocabulary size (|C| vs C_LTA vs queries). For reproducibility, this mapping between encoder class tokens, transcript embeddings A, and decoder queries Q should be more carefully specified.
- The cross-modal attention equations include both a softmax over A WQ (X̂ WK)^T / sqrt(d) + log M and then an additional M^T ⊙ σ(AWg) gating. The masking and gating strategy is quite specific and could be important for performance, but the construction of M (window size, symmetric/asymmetric, use of pseudo-label distributions vs hard argmax) is relegated to “binary local mask” with no details. Given that this is one of the two main technical novelties, the under-specification is a meaningful methodological gap.

**Losses (Sec. 3.2)**

- The ordering of subsections (3.2.3 before 3.2.2 and 3.2.1 in the text) is confusing; but that is editorial, not substantive.
- The ATBA-based loss Latba is described only very briefly and referred to supplementary material. For a paper whose key claim is *alignment from transcripts*, this is not ideal; the reader cannot judge how much of the work is done by ATBA vs the new components.
- For CTC, the formulation is standard; however, the text implies CTC supervises both TAS and the anticipation decoder, but the formula only references the segmentation logits π. It is not clear whether CTC is also applied on anticipated frames (using the full transcript) or only on the observed segment. That distinction matters for how strongly the future predictions are constrained by the transcript.

**Duration Loss**

- The idea of using class-wise duration priors computed from pseudo-label counts is plausible, but the exact momentum update rule, buffer initialization, and handling of rare classes are omitted. These omissions impair reproducibility and make the ablation hard to interpret.

### Experiments

**Datasets & Metrics (Sec. 4.1)**

- Choice of datasets and metrics is standard and appropriate for dense LTA.  
- For EGTEA, evaluation is restricted to verb-only mAP. Given the method uses transcripts that are verb–noun or action-category lists, there is a mild mismatch between training supervision (full action transcript) and evaluation signal (verbs only). This is not fatal but should be clearly acknowledged as a limitation.

**Training & Inference**

- The three-stage training schedule (Lvid pretraining, then LA+LTAS, then full losses) is complex and relies crucially on initial pseudo-label stability. But it is not quantified: no plot of pseudo-label quality vs epochs, no sensitivity analysis to the stages’ lengths. This makes it hard to assess how brittle the method is.
- Importantly, they say “the segmentation head processes the full video during training, while at inference only a fraction is observed”. That means the encoder and head see future frames at train time even though supervision is ostensibly weak. This is acceptable under a standard LTA training protocol but does slightly undermine the narrative that the model must “learn future structures from only observed features”: it actually sees full videos during training; the weakness is in annotation, not exposure.

**Comparative Results (Sec. 4.2, Table 1–2)**

- Baselines for Breakfast and 50Salads are standard and reasonably up-to-date. However, for a claim of “first transcript-only LTA”, it would have been valuable to include **a trivial alignment baseline** (e.g., uniform transcript-to-time mapping, or HMM/CTC-only model) to clarify how much is gained by the proposed architecture vs generic transcript alignment.
- The WS-DA (Zhang et al., 2021) numbers are only partially reported (Breakfast/50Salads at a single setting). There is no discussion of how much of their performance gap can be attributed to the additional fully labeled data they use.

**Ablations (Sec. 4.3, Table 3–4)**

- The ablations do show that CTC, cross-modal attention, CRF, and duration loss each contribute measurable gains on MoC. However, because all these components are stacked, it is difficult to disentangle which are necessary for *weakly supervised* training vs which merely boost any LTA model.  
- No ablation isolates the **effect of transcripts as semantic features** vs transcripts purely as ordering constraints (e.g., by replacing DistilBERT embeddings with learned one-hot label embeddings). Given one of the paper’s claims is semantic grounding, this is a missed but not fatal opportunity.

**Qualitative Results (Sec. 4.4)**

- Qualitative plots are described as visually showing coherent observed segmentation and plausible futures. This is useful but not surprising; qualitative examples do not really address the core issues raised above (supervision regime, duration correctness, etc.).

### Conclusion

- The conclusion restates the “does not need dense annotation” narrative strongly, but without recognizing the significant assumptions and hidden complexities of the ATBA-based alignment and multi-stage training. A more modest framing would be appropriate.

---

## Strengths

- **Novel and important problem formulation:** Explicitly tackling dense LTA with only transcript supervision is a meaningful and under-explored direction. The paper connects weakly supervised TAS ideas (CTC, alignment modules) with LTA in a coherent narrative.
- **Reasonable empirical performance:** On Breakfast in particular, TbLTA achieves strong results, including surpassing some fully supervised baselines (under certain protocols). This is notable given the supervision regime, assuming it is correctly specified.
- **Architectural creativity:** The combination of class tokens, transcript-aware cross-modal attention, a parallel transformer decoder, and a CRF refinement layer is thoughtfully designed for procedural video. The local masking and gated fusion for cross-attention are plausible, interesting ideas.
- **Comprehensive experimentation:** Multiple datasets (Breakfast, 50Salads, EGTEA), multiple observation/prediction horizons, and a nontrivial ablation suite provide a broad empirical picture, even if some crucial details are missing.

---

## Overall Assessment

The paper addresses a genuinely important question—can dense long-term action anticipation be trained from transcripts alone?—and proposes a sophisticated architecture that performs surprisingly well empirically. However, several structural issues undermine the central claims: the supervision regime is not specified clearly enough to substantiate “transcript-only” training; the role and assumptions of the ATBA alignment module and CRF supervision are opaque; and the formal task definition (segment-level anticipation with durations) is not aligned with the actual evaluation, which remains purely framewise. Coupled with somewhat overstated claims of competitiveness with fully supervised baselines, these issues mean that, in its current form, the paper does not convincingly establish its core conceptual contribution. I would not recommend acceptance without a substantial rewriting and re-specification of the supervision assumptions, loss constructions, and evaluation to match the claimed task.
### Neutral Reviewer
## Balanced Review

### Summary
This paper introduces TbLTA, the first weakly-supervised framework for dense long-term action anticipation (LTA) that trains exclusively on video transcripts—ordered action lists without timing or duration information. The model employs an encoder-decoder architecture with a temporal alignment module (ATBA) to generate frame-level pseudo-labels from transcripts, a locally-masked cross-modal attention mechanism to semantically ground video features using transcript embeddings, and a combination of CTC, CRF, and self-supervised duration losses to jointly supervise segmentation and anticipation without dense annotations.

### Strengths
1. **Novel and practical problem formulation.** The paper identifies a genuine gap: while weakly-supervised temporal action segmentation has received growing attention, LTA remains entirely dependent on dense frame-level annotations. Training from transcripts alone represents a substantial reduction in annotation cost and opens a new research direction.
2. **Competitive results on Breakfast.** At 30% observation, the deterministic TbLTA achieves 29.03% average MoC, surpassing all supervised baselines including ActFusion (28.45%). This is a notable result demonstrating that procedural activity structure captured by transcripts can be highly informative for anticipation (Table 1).
3. **Thoughtful cross-modal attention design.** The locally-masked cross-attention (Eq. 1–2) restricts each transcript embedding to attend only to its predicted temporal neighborhood rather than the full video, which is a sensible inductive bias. The ablation in Tables 3–4 confirms consistent gains over unconstrained cross-attention ("simplex") and no cross-attention, with improvements of ~3.8–5.7 points on Breakfast.
4. **Comprehensive ablation study.** The paper systematically evaluates each component (CTC, cross-attention, CRF, duration loss) across both datasets and both tasks (TAS and LTA), making the contribution of each module clear. The CRF ablation particularly highlights its role at longer horizons (~4–5 point drops at 50% prediction).
5. **Progressive training scheme.** The three-stage training (video-level → alignment+segmentation → full objective) is well-motivated by the need for reliable pseudo-label initialization, and the strategy of re-initializing optimizer/scheduler at each stage is a practical detail that aids reproducibility.

### Weaknesses
1. **Substantial performance gap on 50Salads.** The deterministic TbLTA averages 20.92% MoC versus 28.39% for ActFusion—a gap of over 7 points. The paper attributes this to weaker temporal regularities and denser transitions, but does not provide analysis of what transcript-based methods would need to close this gap, or whether the gap is fundamental to the supervision level.
2. **Misleading stochastic evaluation protocol.** The "TbLTA* - Top-1" results (28.51% on 50Salads, 37.15% on Breakfast) report the best sample from multiple stochastic draws, which is not comparable to deterministic baselines that output a single prediction. This inflates numbers and makes cross-method comparison unfair. The "TbLTA* - Mean" results (19.11%, 29.37%) are more honest but less prominently discussed.
3. **Limited architectural novelty.** The core components—ATBA alignment (from Xu & Zheng, 2024), transformer encoder-decoder (from Gong et al., 2022), CRF (from Mate & Dimiccoli, 2024), CTC loss—are all adopted from prior work. The contribution is primarily in the system-level integration rather than individual technical innovation.
4. **Redundancy between CTC and ATBA alignment.** Both CTC loss and ATBA pseudo-labels aim to align transcripts with frame-level predictions, but their complementary roles are not clearly distinguished. The CTC ablation shows only ~0.6–0.8 point gains, raising the question of whether this additional alignment objective is necessary given ATBA already provides pseudo-labels.
5. **Self-supervised duration loss is a weak proxy.** The momentum-based class-wise duration priors (Eq. 7) collapse intra-class variability into a single statistic. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but the ablation shows only marginal gains on 50Salads (~0.2 points), suggesting the duration modeling remains largely unresolved.
6. **Confusing section numbering.** The loss subsections are numbered 3.2.3, 3.2.2, 3.2.1 (reverse order), which makes the logical flow of the objective function presentation difficult to follow.

### Novelty & Significance
The primary novelty lies in the problem formulation—transcript-only supervision for dense LTA—rather than in individual technical components. This is nonetheless significant because it demonstrates feasibility of a much cheaper supervision paradigm and establishes the first baseline for this setting. The significance is bolstered by the competitive results on Breakfast but tempered by the gap on 50Salads and the limited architectural novelty. The work opens a viable research direction but the current approach may need fundamentally new ideas for harder datasets.

### Suggestions for Improvement
1. **Replace or clearly contextualize Top-1 stochastic results.** Either remove the Top-1 reporting or explicitly frame it as an upper-bound oracle, providing the number of samples drawn and the variance across samples to give readers a fair picture.
2. **Deepen analysis on the 50Salads gap.** Provide per-class or per-activity breakdowns to understand whether the gap stems from specific action categories, transition patterns, or duration estimation failures. This would guide future work more effectively.
3. **Clarify the complementary roles of CTC and ATBA.** Since both perform alignment, an ablation removing ATBA while keeping CTC (or vice versa) would help disentangle their contributions and justify the two-stage alignment strategy.
4. **Improve duration modeling.** Consider conditioning duration prediction on the specific activity context (e.g., neighboring actions) rather than only class-wise priors, or explore using the transcript order to inform duration estimates.
5. **Fix section ordering.** Reorder subsections 3.2.1–3.2.3 to follow a logical progression (e.g., alignment → segmentation → anticipation), improving readability.
6. **Add failure case analysis.** Show examples where transcript-based supervision fundamentally fails (e.g., when multiple valid futures exist and the transcript only describes one), which would clarify the inherent limitations of this supervision paradigm.
### Spark
## Howto Improve This Paper

### Missing Experiments (top 3-5 only)
1. **Pseudo-label quality evaluation.** The entire method depends on ATBA pseudo-labels, yet their frame-level accuracy vs. ground truth is never reported. Without this, it is impossible to know whether the framework works because alignment is accurate or despite it being noisy—and whether improvement should focus on alignment or on the downstream components.

2. **Pipeline baseline using existing weakly-supervised TAS.** A natural ablation is: train a weakly-supervised TAS model (e.g., ATBA itself or CLOT) to get pseudo-labels, then train a standard supervised LTA model on those pseudo-labels. This isolates whether the contribution is the end-to-end joint design or simply the availability of pseudo-labels.

3. **Full comparison with WS-DA (Zhang et al., 2021).** The only prior weakly-supervised LTA baseline has a single number reported. Re-implementing and reporting WS-DA across all observation/prediction splits is essential to substantiate the claim of establishing "the first transcript-only baseline."

4. **Robustness to transcript noise/imperfection.** Real transcripts may have missing, swapped, or extraneous actions. No experiment tests how performance degrades with noisy transcripts, which directly undermines the claim that this is a practical, scalable alternative to full supervision.

5. **Ablation of progressive training scheme.** The three-stage training (video-level → segmentation/alignment → full) is presented without ablation. Since pseudo-label quality depends on initialization, removing or altering this scheme could dramatically change results, making it a confound for all other ablations.

### Deeper Analysis Needed (top 3-5 only)
1. **Clarify cross-modal attention at inference.** The transcript (and thus transcript embeddings A) is available during training but not at test time. The paper never states whether cross-attention is disabled, replaced, or how the mask M is constructed without pseudo-labels. This is a critical architectural gap that makes the inference pipeline unclear.

2. **Explain the deterministic-to-stochastic gap.** On 50Salads, deterministic avg is 20.92 but stochastic Top-1 is 28.51—a 36% relative jump. This suggests the deterministic model's raw outputs are poorly calibrated. Analysis of output entropy, calibration, and what "Top-1" selection actually means (best of N samples ranked by what criterion?) is needed to trust these numbers.

3. **Investigate the anomalous Breakfast 30% observation result.** TbLTA deterministic achieves 40.28 at Obs 30% on Breakfast, surpassing all supervised methods (ActFusion: 35.79). This is the paper's strongest claim but also the most suspicious—does the transcript prior simply memorize breakfast procedure structure rather than learn anticipation? A per-class breakdown would clarify this.

4. **Duration prediction quantitative evaluation.** The paper acknowledges duration estimation as a challenge and includes a duration loss, yet provides no metric (e.g., MAE, IoU of predicted vs. ground-truth segment boundaries) to evaluate it. Without this, the duration loss ablation is uninformative.

5. **Analysis of pseudo-label error propagation.** Since pseudo-labels supervise both segmentation and anticipation, systematic alignment errors (e.g., consistently shifted boundaries) could propagate. Analyzing the correlation between pseudo-label accuracy and anticipation accuracy per video would reveal whether the method is robust to alignment noise.

### Visualizations & Case Studies
1. **Pseudo-label vs. ground truth alignment visualization.** Show ATBA pseudo-labels overlaid on ground truth segmentation for multiple videos (both good and bad alignments) to reveal the quality and failure modes of the alignment module that everything else depends on.

2. **Failure case analysis.** The qualitative results show only successful predictions. Showing cases where anticipation fails—especially where pseudo-label alignment is poor—would reveal whether the method's ceiling is bounded by alignment quality.

3. **Deterministic vs. stochastic prediction comparison.** For the same input, visualize multiple stochastic samples alongside the deterministic output to show what diversity the stochastic decoder captures and why Top-1 helps so much.

### Obvious Next Steps
1. **Run a weakly-supervised TAS → supervised LTA pipeline baseline** to isolate the contribution of the joint end-to-end design from the contribution of pseudo-labels alone.

2. **Evaluate pseudo-label frame-level accuracy** as a diagnostic; this should have been a primary result, not omitted.

3. **Explicitly specify the inference procedure for cross-modal attention** when transcripts are unavailable—this is currently ambiguous and likely a reviewer's first question.

### Other stuff you can add
1. **Confidence intervals or standard deviations** across splits are not reported for the main results; adding them would clarify whether differences between TbLTA and supervised methods are statistically meaningful.
2. **EGTEA results are limited** to verb-only mAP with only two supervised baselines; adding more baselines and noun/verb-noun results would strengthen this benchmark.
3. The "stochastic Top-1" protocol needs explicit definition in the main paper (not just supp. mat.)—it currently reads as cherry-picking the best sample without a clear selection criterion.

<strengths_and_weaknesses>

## Strengths

1. **Novel and well-motivated problem formulation**: The paper introduces the first fully weakly-supervised approach for dense long-term action anticipation (LTA), relying solely on video transcripts rather than dense frame-level annotations. This is a meaningful contribution toward making LTA more scalable and practical, as dense annotation is prohibitively costly for long, fine-grained video sequences. This strength aligns with reviewers of AntGPT (Bb21JPnhhr.md) who noted "the question, whether LLMs can assist action anticipation, is surely interesting" and VSNLS reviewers (GQgPj1H4pO.md) who appreciated that "VSNLS addresses the high annotation cost of fully supervised [tasks] by using weak supervision from video captions. This method eliminates the need for extensive manual annotation."

2. **Comprehensive framework with multiple mechanisms**: TbLTA integrates several complementary components—temporal alignment with pseudo-labels, CTC-based transcript supervision, cross-modal attention for semantic grounding, CRF for temporal coherence, and self-supervised duration prediction—into a well-structured encoder-decoder architecture. Each component is justified and ablatively validated.

3. **Strong empirical results on Breakfast**: Under the stochastic (Top-1) protocol, TbLTA achieves 37.15 average MoC on Breakfast, which even surpasses fully-supervised methods like ActFusion (28.45) and FUTR (26.59). On Breakfast with 30% observation, the deterministic model reaches 29.03, exceeding all fully-supervised baselines. This demonstrates that transcript-based supervision can capture procedural regularities effectively.

4. **First transcript-only baseline for LTA**: The paper establishes the first benchmark for this weakly-supervised LTA setting on Breakfast, 50Salads, and EGTEA, which will facilitate future research. This is similar to the contribution recognized by LASER reviewers (HEXtydywnE.md): "This work has high significance as it opens a new path for [task] learning, making it accessible without costly annotation processes."

## Weaknesses

1. **Pseudo-label quality and noise propagation**: The entire framework hinges on the quality of pseudo-labels generated by the ATBA temporal alignment module. Since pseudo-labels are used to supervise both segmentation and anticipation, any systematic errors in alignment—especially around action boundaries—will propagate through the pipeline. The paper acknowledges this ("soft per-frame pseudo-labels that preserve boundary uncertainty") but does not provide a rigorous analysis of pseudo-label quality (e.g., comparing generated pseudo-labels to ground-truth frame labels). As noted in a review of pseudo-label-based methods (DE2RMJVjgI.md): "The generation of pseudo labels by a pre-trained teacher model...can lead to a cascade of errors" and reviewers of weakly-supervised methods (gnWk0ZF22j.md) raised concerns that "the potential limitations and biases introduced by pseudo-labeling" are not "thoroughly addressed." Similarly, a reviewer of the AntGPT paper (Bb21JPnhhr.md) observed that "the proposed method relies on the classification results of previous fragments, and classification errors may lead to the accumulation of errors and affect the prediction results."

2. **Significant gap on 50Salads compared to supervised methods**: The deterministic TbLTA achieves 20.92 average MoC on 50Salads versus ActFusion's 28.39—a substantial ~7.5 point gap. The paper attributes this to "longer videos, denser action distributions, and frequent transitions [that] yield weaker temporal regularities, amplifying the impact of imprecise temporal alignment in the absence of boundary annotations." However, this raises the question of how broadly applicable the approach is beyond datasets with strong procedural structure (like Breakfast). As a VSNLS reviewer (GQgPj1H4pO.md) noted: "It is unclear how well the framework would perform on other [datasets] with different types of actions" and a LASER reviewer (HEXtydywnE.md) raised concerns that "the model seems to have a problem building scene graphs with longer videos and more instances."

3. **Confusing presentation of deterministic vs. stochastic results**: The paper reports results under both deterministic and stochastic protocols in the same table, with the stochastic (Top-1) results being dramatically higher (e.g., 37.15 vs. 29.03 on Breakfast). This conflation makes it difficult to assess the method's true performance and can be misleading, as stochastic sampling multiple predictions and taking the best is a fundamentally different evaluation paradigm. Reviewers of the Actions-to-Action paper (dl34rOnbqJ.md) similarly noted that performance improvements can appear "overselling" when evaluation conditions are not transparent: "our innovative model sets new performance benchmarks: I do not think this is accurate. It seems that the proposed model outperforms competitors by small margins." The paper should more clearly separate and contextualize these two protocols.

4. **Duration estimation remains a major unresolved challenge**: The self-supervised duration loss, based on momentum-based class-wise priors, provides only a "weak duration prior rather than a precise per-instance predictor." The qualitative results and the paper's own conclusion acknowledge that "a major challenge that remains is to correctly estimate future durations, especially for unseen actions." As noted by reviewers of VSNLS (GQgPj1H4pO.md): "Variability in action duration...human actions in video captions unfold over varying duration" makes temporal alignment inherently difficult, and relying on class-averaged duration priors cannot capture intra-class variability.

5. **Limited novelty of individual components**: The CTC loss, cross-modal attention, and CRF are all standard techniques adapted from prior work. The ATBA module is directly adopted from Xu & Zheng (2024), the decoder from Gong et al. (2022b)/Nawhal et al. (2022b), and the CRF from Mate & Dimiccoli (2024). A reviewer of the LASER paper (HEXtydywnE.md) similarly noted: "The reliance on large language models to extract logical specifications may introduce noise and inaccuracies" and questioned whether "training a separate [model] is beneficial" given standard tools. A VSNLS reviewer (GQgPj1H4pO.md) observed that a weakly-supervised framework "does not contribute to any core learning methods...It is mostly a wise tooling over [existing approaches]." While the composition is novel, the architectural novelty of each individual component is limited.

6. **No error analysis of failure cases**: The paper does not include any systematic analysis of when and why the model fails. As an AntGPT reviewer (Bb21JPnhhr.md) noted: "There is no error analysis. When does the proposed method fail and why?" Similarly, a VSNLS reviewer (GQgPj1H4pO.md) flagged the lack of "detailed analysis of failure cases." Understanding failure modes—particularly when pseudo-label alignment goes wrong or when the stochastic protocol produces implausible futures—would strengthen the paper.

7. **Evaluation uses frozen I3D features rather than end-to-end visual learning**: The paper uses pre-extracted 2048-dimensional I3D features as input, meaning the visual encoder is never fine-tuned. While this is common in the TAS/LTA literature, it raises questions about how the approach would perform with more modern visual features or end-to-end training. A VEDIT reviewer (LDAj4UJ4aL.md) raised a related concern about fair comparison: "I cannot find how the baseline [is evaluated], but if it is evaluated with a simple linear classifier...VEDiT's performance gain is just from 'training more parameters on the pre-trained representation.'"

--- Merged Review ---
Now I have enough information for calibration. Let me compile the final review.

## Summary
This paper introduces TbLTA, the first weakly-supervised framework for dense long-term action anticipation (LTA) that trains exclusively on video transcripts—ordered lists of action labels without timing or boundary information. The model uses an encoder-decoder architecture where a temporal alignment module (ATBA) generates frame-level pseudo-labels from transcripts, a locally-masked cross-modal attention mechanism semantically grounds video features using transcript embeddings, and a combination of CTC, CRF, and self-supervised duration losses jointly supervises segmentation and anticipation without dense annotations.

## Strengths
- **Novel and important problem formulation.** Tackling dense LTA with transcript-only supervision is a genuinely new direction. While weakly-supervised TAS has received growing attention, LTA has remained entirely dependent on dense frame-level annotations. Training from transcripts alone represents a substantial reduction in annotation cost (from per-frame labels to ordered action lists) and opens a new research direction. The paper establishes the first baseline for this setting on three standard benchmarks (Breakfast, 50Salads, EGTEA).

- **Strong results on Breakfast.** At 30% observation, deterministic TbLTA achieves 29.03 average MoC on Breakfast, surpassing all fully supervised baselines including ActFusion (28.45). Under the stochastic Top-1 protocol, the advantage is even larger (37.15 vs ~28–29). This demonstrates that for procedurally structured activities, transcript-based supervision captures temporal regularities very effectively.

- **Well-designed cross-modal attention.** The locally-masked cross-attention (Eqs. 1–2) restricts each transcript embedding to attend only to its predicted temporal neighborhood, which is a sensible inductive bias for procedural video. The ablation (Tables 3–4) confirms consistent gains over unconstrained cross-attention ("simplex") and no cross-attention (~3.8–5.7 points on Breakfast).

- **Comprehensive ablation study.** The paper systematically ablates each component (CTC, cross-attention variants, CRF, duration loss) across both datasets and both tasks (TAS and LTA), making the contribution of each module clear. The CRF ablation particularly highlights its role at longer horizons (~4–5 point drops at 50% prediction).

- **Thoughtful progressive training scheme.** The three-stage training (video-level → alignment+segmentation → full objective) is well-motivated by the need for reliable pseudo-label initialization before deploying alignment-based losses, and the strategy of re-initializing optimizer/scheduler at each stage is a practical detail that aids reproducibility.

## Weaknesses

### Major:
- **Inference pipeline is underspecified, particularly for cross-modal attention.** The cross-modal attention (Eqs. 1–2) depends on transcript embeddings A and pseudo-label-derived masking M, both of which require knowing the transcript. During training, the transcript is available, but at inference only observed features Xobs are provided (Sec. 3: "At inference, only [E ∥ Xobs] is provided"). The paper never explicitly states how cross-modal attention operates at test time—whether it is disabled, whether a predicted/sampled transcript is used, or how the mask M is constructed without pseudo-labels. This is a critical gap because cross-attention is one of the two main technical novelties and its ablation shows substantial impact (~3.8–5.7 points on Breakfast). If cross-attention is simply disabled at inference, the model must work well without it, raising questions about what the training-stage cross-attention actually achieves.

- **Stochastic vs. deterministic comparison is misleading.** The paper's most striking numbers—37.15 avg MoC on Breakfast (Top-1 stochastic) vs. ~28.45 for supervised ActFusion (deterministic)—compare fundamentally different evaluation paradigms: stochastic sampling of multiple futures and taking the best vs. single-shot deterministic prediction. The text acknowledges this ("dual view") but the abstract and conclusion emphasize "competitive with, and occasionally superior to" without adequately qualifying that this holds primarily under a different protocol. On Breakfast with deterministic evaluation, TbLTA averages 29.03 vs. ActFusion's 28.45; on 50Salads, deterministic TbLTA is 20.92 vs. ActFusion's 28.39—a ~7.5 point gap. The "competitive" claim is dataset- and protocol-dependent.

- **Substantial performance gap on 50Salads.** Deterministic TbLTA averages 20.92 MoC on 50Salads vs. 28.39 for ActFusion (fully supervised)—a ~7.5 point gap. The paper attributes this to "weaker temporal regularities, amplifying the impact of imprecise temporal alignment," but does not analyze what this means for the broader applicability of transcript-based supervision beyond procedurally structured datasets like Breakfast. This is a significant limitation: the method's performance is closely tied to how strongly procedural the activity is, and the paper should more clearly delineate this boundary.

### Minor:
- **CRF supervision target uses pseudo-labels, not ground truth.** The CRF loss (Eq. 6) is trained on Y_LTA, which the paper calls "the ground-truth anticipation sequence." However, since boundaries are unknown under transcript-only supervision, Y_LTA is derived from ATBA pseudo-labels—itself a noisy allocation of observed vs. future transcript segments. The CRF therefore enforces consistency with an internal pseudo-target rather than true ground truth, which risks reinforcing alignment errors. While this is an inherent limitation of the weak supervision regime, calling it "ground-truth" is technically inaccurate and should be clarified.

- **Duration prediction is unevaluated.** The paper devotes significant architectural and conceptual effort to duration modeling (affinity-based duration loss, momentum buffer, regression head), yet provides no direct evaluation of duration accuracy (e.g., boundary F1, duration error, segment IoU). The ablation (Table 4) shows modest gains (~0.2 on 50Salads, ~3.3 on Breakfast), but these are frame-level MoC metrics, not duration metrics. The qualitative results acknowledge duration estimation as a major challenge. The paper should either evaluate duration directly or more clearly frame the duration module as regularization rather than duration prediction.

- **ATBA's role and training integration are underspecified.** The paper adopts the ATBA module from Xu & Zheng (2024) for temporal alignment but does not clearly specify whether ATBA's parameters are jointly trained with TbLTA or pretrained separately, nor whether it uses any supervision beyond transcripts in this instantiation. Since ATBA is central to the entire pipeline (generating the pseudo-labels that drive both segmentation and anticipation supervision), more clarity on its integration would strengthen confidence that all supervision remains strictly transcript-only.

### Trivial:
- The loss subsection ordering (3.2.3 before 3.2.2 before 3.2.1) is reversed, making the logical flow harder to follow.

## Nice-to-Haves
- **Pseudo-label quality analysis.** Report frame-level accuracy of ATBA pseudo-labels vs. ground truth, which would reveal whether the method works because alignment is accurate or despite it being noisy. This would be one of the most informative diagnostics for the whole approach.
- **Pipeline baseline:** Train a weakly-supervised TAS model separately to generate pseudo-labels, then train a supervised LTA model on those pseudo-labels. This would isolate whether the contribution is the end-to-end joint design vs. simply the availability of pseudo-labels.
- **Noise robustness experiments.** Testing how performance degrades with noisy transcripts (missing, swapped, or extraneous actions) would strengthen the claim that this is a practical, scalable alternative to full supervision.
- **Per-class analysis of the Breakfast anomaly.** The 30% observation result on Breakfast (40.28 Obs 30%) far exceeds supervised baselines—analyzing whether this reflects memorization of procedural structure or genuine anticipation would clarify the method's behavior.

## Removed Points
These points are flagged to be removed, treat them with caution:

- **Harsh Critic's Claim #1 (ATBA introduces stronger-than-transcript supervision):** The harsh critic speculates that ATBA may implicitly encode "stronger supervision than ordered transcript only." However, ATBA (Xu & Zheng, 2024) is explicitly a weakly-supervised method that uses only transcripts for alignment. The paper's progressive training scheme (Lvid pretraining → alignment/segmentation → full objective) is described at sufficient length to understand the bootstrapping process. While more detail on ATBA's integration would be helpful (kept as minor weakness), there is no evidence that the method violates the transcript-only constraint. The concern is speculative without concrete proof of a violation.

- **Harsh Critic's Claim #2 (Task definition / evaluation mismatch):** The critic argues the segment-level formulation with durations isn't evaluated. However, the paper's task definition explicitly says the model predicts both action sequences and durations (Sec. 3), and the evaluation uses the standard dense LTA protocol (frame-level MoC) established by Abu Farha et al. (2018) and used by all prior LTA work. Predicting durations that sum to 1 (Eq. in Sec. 3) is the standard way to convert segment-level predictions to frame-level labels for evaluation. The frame-level MoC metric implicitly evaluates duration correctness (getting durations wrong would yield wrong frame labels). While a direct duration metric would be informative (kept as minor weakness), calling this a "structural mismatch" overstates the issue.

- **Harsh Critic's Claim #3 (CRF not grounded in ground truth):** This is a valid concern but is inherent to any weakly-supervised method and is essentially the same as the minor weakness about CRF pseudo-targets. The harsh critic inflates this to a "structural" issue, but it's the expected consequence of weak supervision—the CRF encourages self-consistency with the best available alignment, which is a reasonable design choice even if imperfect.

- **Harsh Critic's Claim #5 (Duration modeling not demonstrated):** The ablation does show contributions (3.3 points on Breakfast), and the paper acknowledges limitations. The demand for a trivial baseline comparison (e.g., global mean duration) is reasonable as a nice-to-have but not fatal.

- **Neutral Reviewer's "Limited architectural novelty" and Spark's "Redundancy between CTC and ATBA":** System-level integration of existing components into a new task setting is a legitimate form of contribution, especially when establishing the first baseline for a new supervision regime. The CTC ablation shows ~0.6–0.8 point gains, which is modest but not redundant—it provides a different alignment mechanism (marginalization over all paths vs. dynamic programming alignment).

- **Spark's demand for "confidence intervals across splits":** Single-run evaluation with averaged splits is the standard practice in this field. Requesting variance statistics is a nice-to-have, not a core flaw.

## Novel Insights
The paper reveals an interesting asymmetry: transcript-based weak supervision is highly effective for procedurally structured activities (Breakfast) where the temporal ordering is strongly deterministic, but struggles substantially on datasets with weaker procedural structure (50Salads). This suggests transcript supervision captures high-level narrative structure rather than fine-grained temporal dynamics, making it complementary to (rather than a replacement for) frame-level supervision. The Breakfast 30% observation result exceeding supervised baselines is particularly noteworthy—it suggests that for strongly procedural activities, knowing *what* actions occur in order can be more informative than *where* their boundaries are, a finding that could inform future hybrid approaches.

## Suggestions
- Explicitly specify how cross-modal attention operates at inference time (disabled? predicted transcript? fixed mask?), as this is arguably the most important architectural detail left unclear.
- Separate deterministic and stochastic results more clearly in the abstract/conclusion; qualify the "competitive" claim with dataset- and protocol-specific conditions.
- Report pseudo-label accuracy (ATBA alignments vs. ground truth) as a diagnostic—this would be one of the most informative additions.

**Calibration comparison:**

- **AntGPT** (Bb21JPnhhr.md): LTA with LLMs, scores 5/8/6/6 → Accept poster. Similar in being a novel formulation for LTA with limited individual component novelty but strong problem framing. TbLTA is more technically integrated but has the inference underspecification issue.

- **VSNLS** (GQgPj1H4pO.md): Weakly-supervised video understanding via captions, scores 6/6/6/6 → Accept poster. Very similar profile: novel weak supervision formulation, system-level integration, competitive results. TbLTA is comparable in novelty and contribution, though VSNLS doesn't have the inference pipeline gap.

- **LASER** (HEXtydywnE.md): Neuro-symbolic weak supervision for scene graphs, scores 6/6/6/6/6 → Accept poster. Similar: new weak supervision setting, pseudo-label-based, limited individual component novelty, good ablations. TbLTA has stronger results relative to baselines but the inference cross-attention gap and 50Salads weakness are notable.

- **Actions-to-Action** (dl34rOnbqJ.md): Action anticipation with overselling claims, scores 5/3/3/6/5 → Reject. This is weaker than TbLTA in nearly every dimension.

The paper's strengths (genuinely novel problem formulation, strong Breakfast results, good ablations) place it in the 5.5–6.5 range. The inference pipeline underspecification and the misleading stochastic/deterministic comparison pull it down. The 50Salads gap is a real limitation but is acknowledged and somewhat expected for a first baseline in a new setting. I rate it slightly below the VSNLS/LASER papers (which scored 6) due to the inference specification gap, but above a clear borderline paper.

### Harsh Critic
## Critical Issues

### 1. Causal link “self‑derived proposals ⇒ reduced annotation needs” is not actually demonstrated  
**Type: Evidential**  
**Sections:** Abstract, Introduction (end), Contributions bullet (3), Sec. 4.2, Conclusion

The central narrative claim is that generating lesion proposals via GALP “substantially reduces annotation needs” and can act as a surrogate for expert lesion/vessel annotations. The experiments, however, only show that:

- The proposed model, trained and evaluated without *using* external annotations, achieves performance comparable to or slightly better than:
  - older end‑to‑end baselines, and
  - some annotation‑augmented methods (Table 1–3).

What the evidence does *not* show:

- No ablation of GALP “lesion proposals” vs. a comparably strong backbone plus standard CAM pooling or attention; “w/o GALP” in Table 4 throws away both the auxiliary loss and proposal selection at once and then changes LGRF behavior (uses all tokens). This conflates:
  - extra supervision at intermediate layers,
  - spatial sparsification (Top‑K),
  - and the specific CAM‑based proposal design.
- No comparison to simpler self-attention or saliency‑based focus without the expert-routing machinery.
- No experiment that varies the *amount* of external annotation used during training (e.g., partial lesion labels) to show that GALP can reach a given performance with fewer labels than a lesion-supervised baseline.

As a result, the strong story “self‑generated proposals significantly reduce annotation dependence” is only indirectly supported: you introduce a more complex, heavier model, tune it, and find that it can match or slightly exceed prior art that uses external labels. That is consistent with “better backbone + clever fusion beats previous architectures” rather than “self‑derived proposals are an effective annotation surrogate.” The paper needs much more targeted evidence (e.g., controlled label‑efficiency experiments, or at least comparisons to equally powerful end‑to‑end baselines with similar backbones and tokenization) to substantiate this claim. In its current form, the *performance* claims hold, but the central *interpretation* about label efficiency is overstated.

This is not a fatal flaw for the technical contribution, but it does undermine the main narrative.

---

### 2. Fairness and strength of end‑to‑end baselines are not clearly established  
**Type: Evidential / Methodological gap (borderline)**  
**Sections:** Sec. 4.1 (Implementation details), Tables 1–3, 5, Related Work

Your headline comparisons rely heavily on the gap between your method and “end‑to‑end” multi‑view baselines. However:

- Those baselines (MVCINN, ETMC, RETFound, etc.) use a variety of backbones and training recipes from their original papers. Your model is always Swin‑B, pretrained on ImageNet or EyePACS, which is a stronger backbone than several baselines.  
- You do not report a *multi‑view* Swin‑B fusion baseline trained in a comparably strong way (e.g., simple concatenation/attention across views, no GALP/LGRF). The single-view Swin‑B in Table 5 is not a fair multi‑view comparator: it shows that four views help vs. one view, not that your method is better than other possible multi‑view Swin‑based designs.
- On DRTiD, you pretrain on EyePACS “following CrossFiT,” but other end‑to‑end baselines may not benefit from this initialization (and the table suggests most are older CNNs/Transformers with less tailored pretraining).

Because the architecture and pretraining gap are substantial, it is unclear how much of the performance gain over “end‑to‑end” methods comes from GALP+LGRF vs. simply using a modern, high‑capacity backbone with strong pretraining and multi‑view aggregation. This does not invalidate your *absolute numbers* or the SOTA status on DRTiD, but it weakens the attribution of gains to the proposed modules.

To convincingly argue that lesion proposals and expert‑guided fusion are the main driver, there should be at least one strong, Swin‑B‑based multi‑view baseline (e.g., straightforward multi‑view ViT/Swin with cross‑view attention but no GALP/LGRF) reported under the same training protocol.

---

### 3. “Lesion proposals” are assumed but not validated as lesions  
**Type: Evidential**  
**Sections:** Sec. 3.2, Introduction, Conclusion

The method hinges on the interpretation that CAM‑derived Grade Evidence Maps and their Top‑K patches correspond to “lesion proposals” (microaneurysms, exudates, etc.) and serve as internal lesion cues. However:

- There is no quantitative localization evaluation: MFIDDR provides lesion maps; you do not evaluate IoU, recall, or localization quality of proposals against these masks.
- No qualitative figures in the excerpt show whether proposals systematically coincide with lesions vs. general high‑contrast structures or artifacts.
- The auxiliary loss and CAM formulation encourage stage features to be discriminative for *grade*, not necessarily to align with clinically meaningful lesions (grade may also correlate with diffuse vessel changes, overall brightness, etc.).

Without any lesion localization analysis, the term “lesion proposal” is somewhat speculative. The technical mechanism (CAM + Top‑K pooling) is standard and plausible, but the strong interpretation that you are recovering lesion‑level cues in a clinically meaningful way is not substantiated. This matters because that interpretation is used to justify the method as a surrogate for explicit lesion annotations and to claim improved “micro‑lesion sensitivity and interpretability.”

This can be fixed by adding lesion localization experiments, but in the current submission, the lesion‑specific claims are not truly supported.

---

### 4. LGRF / expert routing complexity vs. gain is weakly justified  
**Type: Methodological gap**  
**Sections:** Sec. 3.3, Sec. 4.3, Table 4, hyperparameter study

LGRF introduces substantial complexity: tokenization, cyclic cross‑view routing, an MoE of Transformer experts per stage, load‑balancing loss, and Top‑K expert selection. The ablation in Table 4 shows:

- w/o LGRF: Acc 82.3 vs. 83.9 (∆=1.6%), F1 81.2 vs. 83.5 (∆=2.3%).
- w/o Experts: 82.6/81.4 vs. 83.9/83.5 (∆≈1.3–2.1%).
- w/o GALP: 82.7/82.1 vs. 83.9/83.5 (∆≈1.2–1.4%).

Given dataset sizes (MFIDDR 8.6k eyes), these margins may be real but small. Yet:

- No standard deviation or confidence intervals across repeated runs are provided; it’s unclear if these deltas exceed run‑to‑run variance.
- Computational and memory overhead of per‑stage MoE experts and attention over proposal tokens is not discussed (no FLOPs/latency comparisons).
- The hyperparameter study qualitatively states that α=0.5 and K2=2/M=6 are “best,” but quantitative curves (or tables) are not shown here, and again no variance is reported.

The method might still be acceptable if the main interest is absolute performance, but from a *scientific* perspective, this complexity is not well justified by the magnitude or robustness of the empirical gains.

## Section‑by‑Section Notes

### Introduction

- The staged narrative of DR grading (single‑view → multi‑view → auxiliary signals) is clear and well supported by citations.
- However, the final motivation step implies that reliance on external lesions has become a *fundamental* bottleneck. In practice, some clinical deployments may tolerate that overhead; this could be framed more cautiously as a practical trade‑off rather than a hard ceiling.

### Related Work (Sec. 2)

- Coverage of multi‑view DR grading and annotation‑augmented methods is reasonably thorough.
- It would help to explicitly mention CAM‑based and MoE‑based self‑attention approaches in vision (outside ophthalmology) as conceptual antecedents to GALP and LGRF; at present the narrative may overstate novelty in these mechanism classes.

### Method (Sec. 3)

**GALP (3.2)**

- Auxiliary loss, CAM computation, patch‑level Top‑K, and linear projection are all standard and sufficiently specified for reproduction.
- However, “stage-wise” auxiliary heads are only defined for s1–s3 (Laux sums to n=1..3), implying s4 is purely used for final classification; this design choice is fine but not discussed.
- Claim that “grade evidence in DR is predominantly localized to lesions” is broadly true, but you then treat *all* high‑CAM patches as lesions; this misses potential diffuse or global gradings signals and is not problematized.

**LGRF (3.3)**

- Cross‑view pairing is “adjacent (cyclic)” only. Given four views, there may be relevant non‑adjacent cross‑view correspondences (e.g., view 1 with 3). The choice is not justified; it might be a computational convenience, but the impact is unclear.
- Expert routing uses mean(T^i_sn) as global context. This discards spatial structure, yet the gating is supposed to be region‑aware; rationale is not discussed.
- Load‑balancing loss L_load is borrowed from prior MoE work, but there is no ablation showing whether it matters in this setting.
- The Top‑K2 expert selection has non‑obvious stability implications on small datasets; not discussed.

**Overall training objective (3.4)**

- Hyperparameters λ_aux=1 and λ_load=0.1 are fixed without sensitivity analysis; that is tolerable but could be significant given the small dataset and multiple losses.

### Experiments (Sec. 4)

**Datasets & implementation (4.1)**

- Preprocessing, backbone choice, and patch sizes are reported clearly.
- Using EyePACS pretraining for DRTiD is reasonable but confers a substantial advantage; this should be emphasized when comparing to older baselines.

**Baselines**

- Baseline list is extensive and includes both end‑to‑end and annotation‑augmented methods.
- However, many baselines likely use weaker backbones; you do not include “strong modern transformer baseline with multi‑view attention but no GALP/LGRF,” which is the most relevant for isolating your contribution.

**MFIDDR results (Tables 1–2)**

- Your “w/o lesion” variant is clearly superior to end‑to‑end baselines and on par with several externally informed methods; the numbers are credible.
- But for expert readers, which lesion‑augmented method is truly best is less important than: does a *comparable backbone* without GALP/LGRF perform notably worse? That experiment is missing.
- Per‑grade F1/specificity table is very cluttered (likely a parsing artifact), but it looks like improvements in grade 3 and 4 are modest; again, no confidence intervals.

**DRTiD results (Table 3)**

- You achieve the best Acc and strong AUCs across grades; this supports the claim of SOTA performance on this dataset.
- Still, there is no test‑time annotation use at all in DRTiD for your method, while CrossFiT uses OD/macula coordinates. The claim that you “outperform externally informed methods” is fine, but the implication that this is due to lesion proposals is untested; again, backbone and pretraining alone could explain a lot.

**Ablation and hyperparameters (4.3)**

- The ablation design is sensible in principle (removing GALP, experts, LGRF).
- However, each ablation simultaneously changes multiple aspects:
  - “w/o GALP” both removes proposal selection and changes the input distribution to LGRF (all tokens vs. lesion tokens).
  - “w/o LGRF” replaces cross‑view attention with simple concatenation; a more controlled baseline would keep attention but drop expert routing.
- Hyperparameter study is described qualitatively; quantitative evidence is not shown in the text excerpt, and no robustness analysis is given.

### Appendix

- Table 5, comparing to single‑view Swin, ConvNeXt, PVT, etc., is useful and clearly supports the value of multi‑view modeling in general. It does not isolate GALP/LGRF’s contribution, but it does show that your multi‑view design beats generic single‑view transformers on the same dataset.

## Strengths

- Clear, well‑structured method: GALP (auxiliary CAM‑driven proposals) and LGRF (cross‑view MoE attention) are clearly described, with sufficient mathematical detail for implementation.
- Strong empirical performance: On MFIDDR and DRTiD, your model achieves or surpasses SOTA reported by prior work, and does so without requiring lesion/vessel/OD annotations at inference.
- Extensive baseline coverage: You compare against a broad set of both end‑to‑end and annotation‑augmented methods, plus single‑view baselines, giving a good sense of where your method sits in the existing ecosystem.
- Cross‑view routing idea is interesting: Conditioning expert activation on the current view’s global features to process lesion proposals from another view is a novel twist on MoE‑style routing in multi‑view medical imaging.

## Overall Assessment

The paper presents a technically solid architecture that clearly improves multi‑view DR grading performance over older baselines on two public datasets, and the core mechanisms (CAM‑based proposals + MoE cross‑view attention) are well specified and plausible. However, the most ambitious claims—that self‑derived lesion proposals serve as effective surrogates for lesion annotations, substantially reducing annotation dependence, and that the gains are primarily due to these mechanisms rather than a stronger backbone and pretraining—are not convincingly demonstrated. Absent a strong Swin‑based multi‑view baseline and any quantitative validation of lesion localization, the empirical story supports “a carefully engineered, modern transformer with auxiliary losses achieves new SOTA” more than it supports the specific causal narrative around self‑generated lesion cues. I would not reject this as “fundamentally flawed”—the method works and is nontrivial—but in its current form it overclaims on annotation efficiency and interpretability. For acceptance at a top venue, I would expect additional experiments that (i) control for backbone strength, (ii) validate lesion proposals against available masks, and (iii) more cleanly isolate GALP and LGRF’s contributions.
### Neutral Reviewer
## Balanced Review

### Summary
The paper proposes an end-to-end framework for multi-view diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading that eliminates the need for costly external annotations (lesion maps, vessel masks, OD/macula coordinates). The Grade-Activated Lesion Proposal (GALP) module generates self-derived lesion proposals on-the-fly via class-activation maps from auxiliary classifiers, while the Cross-View Lesion Expert-Guided Regional Fusion (LGRF) module uses a Mixture-of-Experts routing mechanism to selectively fuse lesion-salient information across views. Experiments on two multi-view DR benchmarks show the method matches or surpasses externally-informed baselines without additional annotations.

### Strengths
1. **Clear and practical motivation**: The paper identifies a real deployment bottleneck—existing multi-view DR methods depend on expensive external annotations—and proposes a clean solution that maintains end-to-end training while achieving comparable performance. The argument that annotation-dependent methods create workflow burden and system brittleness is well-articulated (Section 1, "Switch = On/Off" framing).

2. **Strong empirical results without external annotations**: The lesion-free variant achieves 83.9% accuracy on MFIDDR, surpassing all end-to-end baselines and several externally-informed methods (e.g., LFMVDR with lesion at 82.2%, CVSA with vessel at 82.6%). On DRTiD, 76.0% accuracy exceeds all compared methods including the externally-informed CrossFiT (75.6%). This directly validates the central claim.

3. **Well-structured ablation study**: Table 4 provides clean isolation of each component's contribution. Removing GALP drops accuracy by 1.2%, removing experts by 1.3%, and removing LGRF entirely by 1.6%, confirming that each module plays a complementary role.

4. **Per-grade performance analysis**: Table 2 reveals that the method excels on clinically challenging grades—particularly Grade 3 (F1=74.1% without lesions, 74.8% with lesions, both best-in-class)—demonstrating genuine improvement in detecting moderate-to-severe DR rather than just inflating Grade 0 accuracy.

5. **The GALP design is elegant**: Using normalized CAMs from stage-wise auxiliary classifiers to derive evidence maps, then applying top-K region selection, is a principled way to obtain spatial proposals without any extra supervision. The design strengthens intermediate representations while simultaneously generating useful spatial cues.

### Weaknesses
1. **No qualitative validation of lesion proposals**: The paper's core assumption is that GALP-derived evidence maps correspond to actual lesions. This is never verified. Without visualization comparing GALP proposals against ground-truth lesion annotations (which MFIDDR provides), it is impossible to assess whether the method truly "recovers small, low-contrast lesions" as claimed, or whether high-activation regions correspond to artifacts, the optic disc, or other non-lesion structures. This is a critical gap for a method whose central contribution is self-derived lesion proposals.

2. **Interpretability claim is unsupported**: The contributions list "superior robustness and interpretability," but no attention visualizations, expert routing analyses, or qualitative examples are provided anywhere in the paper. Without such evidence, this claim cannot be evaluated.

3. **No computational cost analysis**: The LGRF module introduces M=6 Transformer experts with MoE routing, multi-head cross-view attention, and stage-wise processing across four stages. No FLOPs, parameter counts, or inference time comparisons are reported, making it impossible to assess the practical trade-off between accuracy gains and computational overhead.

4. **Limited statistical rigor**: Results are reported as single runs without standard deviations or confidence intervals. Given that some improvements over baselines are modest (e.g., 83.9 vs. 83.0 for SMVDR-W on MFIDDR), it is unclear whether differences are statistically significant.

5. **Cyclic adjacent-view fusion is restrictive**: The fusion strategy only considers adjacent (cyclic) views. In the 4-view setting, non-adjacent view pairs (e.g., view 1 and view 3) may contain complementary lesion evidence that is never directly exchanged. The paper does not justify this design choice or experiment with alternatives.

6. **Numerous hyperparameters with limited sensitivity analysis**: The method introduces K₁, K₂, M, α, q, λ_aux, λ_load. While Fig. 3 explores some, the full hyperparameter space is not systematically covered, raising concerns about tuning difficulty and generalizability.

### Novelty & Significance
The paper offers moderate novelty. Using CAM-based spatial proposals from auxiliary classifiers is not new in general (CAM-based attention/selection has appeared in many contexts), but the specific application to generating self-supervised lesion proposals for multi-view DR grading is well-motivated and the GALP+LGRF combination is novel. The MoE-based cross-view expert routing conditioned on the current view's context is a meaningful design contribution. The practical significance is high: demonstrating that internally generated proposals can replace costly external annotations makes the method far more deployable in clinical settings. The significance is somewhat tempered by the lack of qualitative validation that the proposals actually correspond to lesions.

### Suggestions for Improvement
1. **Add qualitative visualizations**: Overlay GALP evidence maps and top-K selected regions on fundus images alongside ground-truth lesion annotations. This is essential to validate the fundamental assumption and would significantly strengthen the paper.

2. **Report computational costs**: Provide FLOPs, parameter counts, and inference times for the proposed method versus key baselines (e.g., MVCINN, CVSA). This is critical for clinical deployment claims.

3. **Add statistical significance**: Run experiments with multiple seeds and report mean ± standard deviation, or at minimum perform significance tests against the strongest baselines.

4. **Explore non-adjacent view fusion**: Ablate the cyclic adjacency constraint versus full pairwise fusion to justify the design choice and assess whether cross-view information is being lost.

5. **Include expert routing analysis**: Visualize which experts are activated for different views/grades and what each expert specializes in. This would substantiate the interpretability claim and provide insight into the model's decision-making.

6. **Discuss failure cases**: Analyze where the method fails (e.g., which grades/views are most commonly confused) and discuss limitations more openly, including the inherent limitation that CAM-based proposals may be coarse for very small lesions like microaneurysms.
### Spark
## How to Improve This Paper

### Missing Experiments (top 3-5 only)
1. **Quantitative evaluation of lesion proposal quality against ground truth**: MFIDDR provides lesion segmentation masks, yet the paper never measures whether GALP proposals actually localize real lesions (e.g., IoU, hit rate). Without this, the core claim that "self-generated proposals act as surrogates for expert cues" is unsubstantiated — the gains could come entirely from the auxiliary classification loss rather than from meaningful lesion localization.

2. **Ablation separating auxiliary loss from proposals**: The current ablation removes GALP entirely. A critical missing condition is: keep the auxiliary classification loss but replace top-K CAM-based proposals with random region selection. If this performs similarly, the "lesion proposal" mechanism is not doing what is claimed.

3. **Statistical significance reporting**: No standard deviations or multiple runs are reported. With small medical datasets, single-run results are unreliable. Add mean±std over at least 3 seeds to confirm the claimed improvements are not due to variance.

4. **Cross-view fusion topology ablation**: The method only fuses adjacent (cyclic) views. For 4-view data, non-adjacent views (e.g., view 1 and view 3) may carry complementary lesion evidence. An ablation comparing cyclic vs. all-pairs fusion would clarify whether the adjacency assumption is justified or limiting.

### Deeper Analysis Needed (top 3-5 only)
1. **Per-grade error analysis on where and why the method fails**: The paper claims to recover "small, low-contrast lesions" but provides no analysis of failure modes. Are microaneurysms (Grade 1) still missed? Does the method systematically underperform on specific grade transitions?

2. **Expert specialization analysis**: The MoE routing is claimed to "selectively activate experts" based on cross-view context, but there is no analysis of whether different experts specialize in different lesion types or spatial patterns. Visualizing routing patterns across grades would validate or invalidate this claim.

3. **Computational overhead analysis**: No FLOPs, parameter count, or training/inference time comparison is provided. The expert pool, routing network, and multi-stage processing add non-trivial overhead; readers cannot assess practical trade-offs.

### Visualizations & Case Studies
1. **GEM/lesion proposal overlays on input images**: The paper derives Grade-conditioned Evidence Maps but never visualizes them. Overlaying top-K selected regions on fundus images alongside ground truth lesion masks would directly show whether proposals correspond to real lesions — this is the single most important visualization for validating the method.

2. **Cross-view proposal correspondence examples**: Show lesion proposals from multiple views of the same eye to demonstrate that the cross-view expert gating identifies corroborating regions across views vs. ignoring irrelevant ones.

3. **Failure case gallery**: Show cases where the method misgrades, with GEM overlays, to reveal systematic blind spots (e.g., peripheral lesions, low-contrast microaneurysms).

### Obvious Next Steps
1. **Quantify proposal quality using available MFIDDR lesion masks**: Compute IoU/hit-rate of top-K CAM regions against ground truth segmentations to directly test whether proposals localize lesions.

2. **Report results with multiple random seeds and standard deviations**: Standard practice for medical imaging papers; required for trust.

3. **Add the auxiliary-loss-only + random-regions ablation**: This is the most informative missing ablation for isolating the contribution of the proposal mechanism itself.

### Other stuff you can add
1. **Clarify what "with lesion" means operationally**: The SPADE-based lesion fusion variant is mentioned briefly but not detailed. If it's a key comparison row, the mechanism deserves explicit description.
2. **Discuss limitations of CAM-based proposals**: CAMs are known to highlight only the most discriminative regions and may miss diffuse or subtle lesion patterns — this limitation should be acknowledged.
### Human Finder
Based on my review of the paper and relevant human-written reviews, here are the identified strengths and weaknesses:

## Strengths

1. **Well-motivated problem formulation**: The paper clearly identifies the practical limitations of externally-informed multi-view DR grading methods (annotation cost, workflow burden, upstream model coupling) and proposes a principled end-to-end alternative that self-generates lesion proposals, which is a meaningful contribution toward reducing annotation dependency in clinical settings.

2. **Competitive performance without external annotations**: Achieving 83.9% accuracy on MFIDDR and 76.0% accuracy on DRTiD without any external annotations, matching or exceeding methods that require costly expert annotations, is a strong practical result.

3. **Thorough ablation study**: The paper provides ablation experiments for GALP, LGRF, and expert components (Table 4), as well as hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for K1, K2, and M (Fig. 3), demonstrating the contribution of each module.

## Weaknesses

1. **No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported**: The paper reports single performance numbers without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple-run statistics. Multiple reviewers of similar MoE-based medical imaging methods (e.g., M4oE) raised this concern: *"Are the performance improvements significant? Can you conduct significance testing and provide confidence intervals?"* and *"No confidence intervals or standard deviation of results are reported to judge the statistical significance of the results."* — [NJxCpMt0sf.md, Reviewer 2 & Reviewer 4]. Given the small performance margins (e.g., 83.9% vs. 83.0% for SMVDR-W), statistical significance is critical to validate claims of SOTA competitiveness.

2. **Quality and reliability of self-derived CAM-based lesion proposals is not verified**: The GALP module derives lesion proposals from Grade-Activated Evidence Maps (CAMs), which are well-known to be noisy, imprecise, and prone to highlighting discriminative but non-lesion regions. The paper does not provide any quantitative evaluation (e.g., IoU, precision/recall) of whether the Top-K selected regions actually correspond to ground-truth lesion locations, even though MFIDDR provides lesion segmentation masks. Reviewers of CAM-based weakly supervised methods have raised this concern: *"What if the GradCAM does not provide good initializations or even wrong saliency maps? What are the effects of inaccurate saliency map creation on the quality of the pseudo-labels generated by the proposed method?"* — [RJDjSXNuAZ.md, Reviewer 2], and *"the segmentation performance might be closely tied to the quality of heatmaps... How robust is this method to such real-world scenarios with dataset and class imbalances?"* — [3b8CgMO5ix.md, Reviewer 3]. Without such validation, the claim that these are "lesion proposals" is unsupported.

3. **Computational cost and runtime overhead not discussed**: The framework introduces stage-wise auxiliary classifiers, CAM computation, Top-K proposal selection, expert pools (M=6), Top-K2 routing, and multi-head cross-view attention at every stage—adding substantial computational overhead. Yet no FLOPs, parameter counts, training/inference time, or comparison with baselines is provided. Reviewers of similar MoE-based medical methods flagged this: *"The M4oE framework is complex, raising concerns about optimization and practical implementation. Including a discussion on computational resources and runtime would help readers assess its feasibility for real-world applications"* — [NJxCpMt0sf.md, Reviewer 1], and *"Please discuss the computational cost compared to the baselines"* — [NJxCpMt0sf.md, Reviewer 3].

4. **Hyperparameter sensitivity and expert configuration not thoroughly analyzed**: The paper has many interdependent hyperparameters (α=50%, K2=2, M=6, q=7/8, λaux=1, λload=0.1). While Fig. 3 shows sensitivity to α, K2, and M individually, there is no joint sensitivity analysis or principled justification for the chosen configurations. Reviewers of MoE-based methods asked: *"Is there an ablation study for a reduced number of experts? How sensitive is this method when the number of experts decreases compared to other MoE methods? What is the procedure for choosing the number of experts?"* — [NJxCpMt0sf.md, Reviewer 3], and *"What was your hyperparameter tuning strategy? It is unclear if these baselines have been best optimized"* — [NJxCpMt0sf.md, Reviewer 4].

5. **Limited evaluation scope—only two DR datasets, both small to medium**: The paper evaluates on MFIDDR (8,613 eyes) and DRTiD (3,100 eyes), both for the same DR grading task. No evaluation on more diverse medical imaging tasks, different disease types, or datasets with different characteristics (e.g., severe class imbalance, different numbers of views) is provided. Reviewers of similar specialized medical methods noted: *"The paper lacks a discussion on its generalizability across diverse medical imaging modalities and less common diseases"* — [8g5Ye3c3oR.md, Reviewer 2], and *"The method is evaluated on only virus detection in electron microscopy images... the method may not generalize to object detection in other microscopy imaging modalities"* — [RJDjSXNuAZ.md, Reviewer 2].
