--- Merged Review ---
## Summary

The paper proposes an end-to-end multi-view diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading framework that avoids relying on external lesion/vessel/OD annotations at inference. It introduces (i) Grade-Activated Lesion Proposals (GALP), which uses stage-wise auxiliary classifiers and CAMs to derive top-K grade-evidence regions as tokens, and (ii) Lesion-expert Guided Regional Fusion (LGRF), which routes cross-view lesion tokens through a mixture-of-experts module and Top-K–weighted cross-view attention. On two multi-view DR benchmarks (MFIDDR, DRTiD), the method outperforms prior end-to-end baselines and is competitive with several annotation-augmented methods.

## Strengths

- **Clear, well-specified architecture.**  
  The design of GALP and LGRF is mathematically explicit: auxiliary heads with focal loss, CAM-based evidence maps, patch aggregation into proposal tokens, MoE-style cross-view expert routing, and Top-K–weighted cross-view attention are all described in enough detail to reproduce.

- **Strong empirical performance as an end-to-end baseline.**  
  On MFIDDR, “Ours (w/o lesion)” reaches 83.9% Acc, 89.8% Spec, 70.9% Kappa, and 83.5% F1, outperforming all listed “End-to-End” multi-view methods and even surpassing some externally informed baselines (e.g., CVSA with vessel, LFMVDR with lesions). On DRTiD, their end-to-end variant attains the best reported accuracy (76.0%), slightly exceeding CrossFiT (75.6%) and CVSA (74.7).

- **Reasonable ablation demonstrating utility of the proposed modules.**  
  On MFIDDR (Table 4), removing GALP, the experts, or LGRF each reduces performance (Acc from 83.9 to 82.7, 82.6, and 82.3, respectively), indicating that both the CAM-based proposal mechanism and the cross-view expert fusion contribute beyond a Swin-B backbone alone.

- **Flexibility to integrate external lesion information.**  
  The same architecture can incorporate lesion segments via SPADE, yielding “Ours (with lesion)” at 84.6% Acc and 72.3% Kappa on MFIDDR, which is competitive with or slightly better than prior lesion-augmented models. This supports the claim that the framework is adaptable when annotations are available, while not requiring them at inference.

- **Thorough baseline coverage including multi-view and single-view.**  
  The paper compares against a wide set of multi-view methods (MVCINN, ETMC, CrossFiT, etc.) and provides an appendix table showing substantial margins over strong single-view backbones (ConvNeXt, Swin-B, ViM, PVT), underlining the value of both multi-view input and the proposed fusion strategy.

## Weaknesses

### Fatal

None. The paper presents a coherent method, correct formulations, and meaningful empirical gains. The main issues concern overclaiming and missing validation/analysis, not fundamental methodological flaws.

### Major

- **Overclaiming on “substantially reducing annotation needs” without quantitative evidence.**  
  The central narrative is that self-derived proposals “substantially reduce annotation needs” and act as surrogates for expensive lesion/vessel/OD labels (Abstract, Intro, Contributions (1)(3), Conclusion). What is *actually* demonstrated is: a strong end-to-end model, trained using only DR grades, achieves performance close to or slightly above some methods that were *trained* with additional annotations. The paper does not:
  - Quantify annotation cost vs. performance, or show performance as a function of label budget.
  - Compare against a strong backbone plus standard training (e.g., Swin-B + simple fusion) under the same grade-only supervision to isolate GALP’s contribution relative to “just using a better backbone.”
  - Analyze how much closer GALP brings performance to the “with lesion” variant than a backbone-only model does.
  
  As a result, the idea that annotation needs are “substantially reduced” is currently qualitative. A more accurate claim is that an annotation-free model is *competitive* with annotation-augmented baselines; the stronger resource-efficiency framing is not quantitatively supported.

- **No validation that “lesion proposals” correspond to true lesions, despite available masks.**  
  GALP assumes top-K CAM-derived regions are lesion proposals and repeatedly uses lesion-centric language (“lesion-aware cues”, “recovering small, low-contrast lesions”, “micro-lesion sensitivity”). Yet:
  - MFIDDR comes with lesion segmentation masks (they are even used to build “Ours (with lesion)”), but there is no experiment measuring spatial overlap, recall, or precision of GALP proposals against these ground-truth lesions.
  - There is no comparison to CAMs from a vanilla Swin-B backbone to show that GALP’s proposals are more lesion-faithful than standard attention maps.
  - All reported gains are at the *grade* level; they can be explained by better global discriminative representations without requiring improved lesion localization.
  
  Therefore, the semantic interpretation of proposals as “lesions” and the claim of improved “micro-lesion sensitivity” are not substantiated. The work does show that CAM-guided token selection improves grading, but the lesion-localization story should be either validated or substantially softened.

- **Fairness of SOTA comparisons is under-argued, especially w.r.t. backbone capacity and training setup.**  
  The method uses Swin-B, a high-capacity transformer, while many baselines are older CNNs or smaller networks (ResNet, VGG, MVCINN). The paper acknowledges different pretraining (ImageNet vs EyePACS) to match some baselines, but does not:
  - Clarify whether any externally informed methods were re-implemented on the same backbone or under identical data augmentations and training pipelines.
  - Detail hyperparameters (LR, optimizer, data augmentation, epochs, batch size) needed to judge whether the training regime is more intensive or favorable.
  - Discuss whether differences in backbone size alone could account for part of the margin over older methods.
  
  This does not negate that the model is strong, but it weakens the force of “new SOTA” when the architecture and backbone differ substantially from prior work. More cautious wording (“competitive with SOTA under typical backbones”) or controlled re-implementations would make the comparative claims more solid.

- **Lesion-expert MoE routing is not well justified relative to simpler alternatives.**  
  LGRF adds nontrivial complexity: routing scores from current-view tokens, top-K2 expert selection, load-balancing loss, and per-expert Transformer processing of lesion tokens. The only ablation is “w/o Experts,” which reduces accuracy from 83.9% to 82.6% (a ~1.3 point drop). The paper does not:
  - Compare against a single non-expert Transformer block with similar parameter count.
  - Ablate the load-balancing loss (λ_load) or report whether experts collapse or specialize.
  - Provide any analysis of routing patterns or expert roles.
  
  Thus, while the MoE component appears to help modestly, the claims around “dynamic expert routing” and “context-aware expert selection” are not backed by diagnostic experiments. This undercuts the architectural rationale for using MoE instead of simpler attention-based fusion.

### Minor

- **Lesion/grade semantics are overstated relative to the available evidence.**  
  The text repeatedly presents DR grade as “predominantly determined by lesion evidence” and equates high CAM activations to lesion regions. In practice, CAMs can highlight broader regions, vascular patterns, or artifacts that correlate with grade without being lesions per se. The paper does not acknowledge these limitations or discuss potential non-lesional correlates; adding such nuance would make the mechanistic narrative more realistic.

- **No statistical variability or significance analysis.**  
  All metrics appear to be from single runs, with relatively small margins over some strong baselines (e.g., Acc 76.0 vs 75.6 on DRTiD; various 1–2 point differences in F1). Without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or repeated runs, it is unclear which gains are robust vs. within noise.

- **Limited discussion of generalization and missing-view scenarios.**  
  The method is evaluated on two fundus datasets with fixed numbers of views (4 and 2). There is no discussion of how the cyclic adjacency fusion would extend to variable numbers of views, missing views, or other imaging modalities. This does not invalidate the method but narrows its demonstrated scope.

- **Training details are incomplete.**  
  Key ingredients like optimizer choice, learning rate schedule, number of epochs, batch size, and augmentation strategies are omitted. While common in some vision papers, this omission makes exact reproduction and fair hyperparameter comparison harder.

- **Some design choices are under-motivated.**  
  For example, restricting cross-view fusion to adjacent (cyclic) views is unusual; no rationale or ablation against all-pairs fusion is provided. Similarly, the fixed retention ratio α=50% and fixed M=6 experts are chosen based on a brief hyperparameter study on a single dataset; more discussion would help justify these as generally good settings.

### Trivial

- Occasional typos and minor notational artifacts from PDF extraction (e.g., “whcih”, duplicated equations labels) but these are clearly parsing issues and do not affect scientific content.
- The statement in Related Work that auxiliary-annotation methods “break end-to-end training” is imprecise; many of them remain end-to-end w.r.t. their own modules. This is wording rather than a technical flaw.

## Nice-to-Haves

- **Direct quantitative evaluation of proposal–lesion overlap.**  
  Using MFIDDR’s lesion masks to compute IoU/recall of GALP proposals vs. true lesions (stratified by lesion type and grade) would strongly support or refine the lesion-proposal interpretation.

- **More granular ablation of GALP’s components.**  
  An ablation that separates: (a) auxiliary heads only (no Top-K proposal selection) vs. (b) proposal selection without auxiliary loss vs. (c) full GALP would clarify whether gains come from better supervision, token pruning, or both.

- **Computational cost and resource usage.**  
  Reporting FLOPs, parameter counts, and (approximate) inference time for the full model vs. simpler baselines would help readers judge its deployability in large-scale screening.

- **Cross-dataset robustness.**  
  A train-on-one / test-on-the-other experiment (MFIDDR→DRTiD or vice versa) would give some sense of how well the CAM-based proposals generalize across acquisition protocols.

## Removed Points

These points are flagged to be removed or de-emphasized; treat them with caution.

- **Criticism that the paper does not prove CAMs are “the actual mechanism” of the model’s decisions.**  
  This kind of argument, imported from some CAM literature, is not directly applicable here: the authors only *use* CAMs to construct proposals; they do not claim CAMs perfectly match the decision process. The real gap is lack of lesion overlap evaluation, which is already captured in a major weakness above.

- **Generic complaints about missing “all” training details or code as a reproducibility failure.**  
  While more detail would be beneficial, the method and losses are sufficiently specified for a competent practitioner to reimplement. Under the venue’s norms, this is a minor, not fatal, issue.

- **Assertions that evaluation is “unfair” because some baselines use external annotations.**  
  The paper clearly separates end-to-end vs. externally-informed methods and does not hide that some baselines have more supervision. The legitimate concern is backbone/tuning parity, which is already addressed as a major weakness.

- **Claims that resizing images necessarily destroys micro-lesion information to the point of invalidating results.**  
  The authors follow prior work’s resizing and preprocessing protocols; without contrary evidence, this should not be treated as a critical flaw.

## Novel Insights

The main genuinely novel insight is that, in multi-view DR grading, a straightforward combination of stage-wise CAM-guided token selection and cross-view fusion can substantially close the gap between pure grade-supervised models and prior systems that rely on explicit lesion/vessel/OD annotations. The experiments suggest that much of the benefit of lesion guidance can be approximated by internal proposal mechanisms, even without lesion-level supervision, though the lesion semantics need more validation. The MoE-based fusion appears to offer modest additional gains, but its specific contribution beyond extra capacity is less clear.

## Suggestions

- Temper the central claims to match the evidence: emphasize that the method is a strong end-to-end multi-view grader competitive with annotation-augmented baselines, and describe annotation reduction qualitatively unless you add annotation–performance tradeoff experiments.
- Use MFIDDR’s lesion masks to quantitatively evaluate how well GALP proposals correspond to true lesions (recall at various K, overlap by lesion type). This would either validate or appropriately constrain the lesion-centric interpretation.
- Add a more diagnostic ablation for GALP and LGRF:
  - Separate auxiliary loss vs. token selection effects in GALP.
  - Compare MoE fusion to a single Transformer block with similar parameters; ablate the load-balancing loss.
- Provide basic runtime and complexity numbers (parameters, FLOPs, approximate inference time per eye) and discuss whether the additional complexity is acceptable in realistic screening workflows.
- Include at least high-level training details (optimizer, learning rate schedule, batch size, epochs, augmentation). If possible, clarify which baselines were re-trained under your pipeline vs. copied from the literature, and note differences in backbones explicitly when claiming SOTA.
- Add qualitative visualizations of evidence maps and selected proposals overlaid with lesion masks for representative cases (true positives and failures), to give readers intuition about what GALP is focusing on.

Regarding the standard axes:

- **Originality:** Moderate. Components (CAMs, auxiliary heads, MoE) are known; the novelty is in their specific integration for annotation-free multi-view DR grading.
- **Importance of question:** High within medical imaging: reducing reliance on lesion-level annotations in DR grading is practically valuable.
- **Support for claims:** Strong for “better end-to-end performance” and “competitive with externally-informed methods”; weak for “substantially reduce annotation needs” and “micro-lesion sensitivity/lesion proposals” without lesion-level validation.
- **Soundness of experiments:** Generally sound but missing statistical variability, cost analysis, and lesion-overlap evaluation.
- **Clarity of writing:** Good to very good; some over-enthusiastic wording and minor notational clutter, but overall understandable.
- **Value to the community:** Solid, especially as a strong end-to-end baseline and as a design pattern (CAM-guided token selection + cross-view fusion) that could be reused in other multi-view medical settings.

## Score and Decision

Calibration (conceptual, given limited direct access to other reviews):

- Compared to moderately strong but somewhat incremental MoE/medical imaging papers (typically scoring around 5–6), this work has clearer empirical gains and a well-motivated clinical problem, but also notable overclaiming and missing validation of its key “lesion proposal” story.
- It is clearly above papers that are fundamentally flawed or non-reproducible (scores ≤3), and somewhat below truly polished, rigorously validated SOTA works with thorough analysis (scores ≥8).

Given the balance of strong empirical results and significant but fixable evidential gaps, I place this paper in the “borderline but leaning accept if claims are tempered / additional validation added” range.

### Harsh Critic
## Critical Issues

### 1. Spectral-bias alleviation is only heuristically (not rigorously) established  
**Type: Evidential / partly Structural**  
**Sections: 3 (spectral bias), 4 (SepPGD), Lemma 2, Remark after Lemma 2, experiments**

The central algorithmic claim is that SepPGD “provably adjusts the eigenvalue distribution of [the] NTK matrix, effectively alleviating spectral bias of SepNNs,” with convergence advantages over standard GD/PGD.

However:

- The proof that SepPGD improves the NTK spectrum is incomplete and largely heuristic:

  - Lemma 2 only establishes algebraic equivalence between SepPGD and a specific NTK-based PGD with preconditioner  
    \(\tilde S = S_1\otimes I_n + I_n\otimes S_2\) (bivariate case), under a specific construction of factor preconditioners.  

  - The crucial step—showing that the eigenvalues of \(K \tilde S\) are better conditioned than those of \(K\)—is not actually proved. The text says “This can possibly be verified” and then sketches qualitative reasoning about Kronecker products and the fact that each \(S_d\) has “better spectrum” than \(K_{\Theta_d}\). There is no theorem, no concrete bound, and no clear statement of conditions under which the global NTK \(K\) is close to the surrogate \( \tilde K = K_{\Theta_1}\otimes I + I\otimes K_{\Theta_2}\).

  - In higher‑dimensional cases \(D>2\), the paper explicitly leaves extension of Lemma 2 and convergence analysis to “future research”, yet the abstract and introduction claim general spectral-bias alleviation for multivariate SepNNs.

- The link between **factor NTKs** and the **true SepNN NTK** is underdeveloped. Lemma 1 expresses the NTK in terms of factor NTKs and multiplicative “a_d(x)” weights, but Section 4 then assumes (without proof) that a block‑Kronecker NTK \(\tilde K\) built from per-dimension NTKs is an adequate surrogate for \(K\). All spectrum arguments about \(K \tilde S\) are made via this surrogate.

- The theoretical guarantees from Geifman et al. (2024) apply to preconditioners carefully constructed from the **true NTK**; here, SepPGD uses **factor NTKs** as proxies. There is no formal statement that the corresponding kernel ridge regression solution and convergence rates still match the target GD solution on the original SepNN.

Given how central the “provably adjusts the eigenvalue distribution … effectively alleviating spectral bias” claim is, this gap is serious. In its current form, the paper offers a plausible algorithm with convincing **empirical** evidence and some algebraic equivalence in low‑D, but not a rigorous theoretical guarantee of spectral-bias alleviation for general SepNNs. The core theoretical selling point is overstated relative to what is actually proved.

### 2. NTK regime analysis limited to an unrealistic asymptotic that does not match the intended use of SepNNs  
**Type: Evidential**  
**Sections: 3 (Theorem 2, Corollary 1, Remark 2), discussion around fixed rank**

The NTK analysis is used to support claims about training dynamics and spectral bias of SepNNs. But:

- The main deterministic NTK result (Theorem 2) assumes **both width \(W \to \infty\)** and **rank \(R \to \infty\)**. This is precisely the regime *not* used in practice; as the authors themselves emphasize, in real applications the rank is chosen small to improve generalization and efficiency.

- For the **practical regime** (fixed small rank and \(W\to\infty\)), the paper only proves that the NTK converges **in distribution to a random kernel** (Corollary 1). They explicitly note that in this setting “the training dynamic can not be characterized uniformly using a fixed NTK matrix as in (5) due to the randomness,” and the possible stochastic-differential-equation analysis is left as “promising future directions”.

- Despite this, the subsequent discussion of spectral bias and SepPGD is framed using the **deterministic NTK dynamics** (equation (5)), where eigenvalues of a fixed NTK matrix govern convergence. There is no attempt to reconcile how these deterministic-spectral-bias arguments translate to the random‑NTK setting of fixed rank, which is where SepPGD is supposed to matter most.

- The experiments all use finite, often relatively small ranks; there is no attempt to relate empirical spectra or dynamics to the random‑NTK limit or to check whether the deterministic NTK approximation is at all valid in those regimes.

Thus the paper’s theoretical characterization of spectral bias is rigorous only in a limit (infinite rank) that conflicts with the very motivation for using SepNNs. For the regime that actually matters, the analysis is incomplete and the paper slides back into using the deterministic NTK story without justification. This does not completely invalidate the empirical findings, but it does mean that the “NTK regimes and spectral bias characterization” contribution is only partially delivered.

### 3. Universal approximation theorem contributes limited novelty over known results  
**Type: Methodological gap (weighting / contribution positioning)**  
**Section: 2 (Theorem 1, discussion)**

The universal approximation result is technically correct and nicely presented, but its substantive contribution is weaker than the abstract/introduction imply:

- For CP architectures, the density of finite sums of products of univariate continuous functions on rectangular domains is classical (Stone–Weierstrass). The proof sketch indeed just recycles this plus the standard universal approximation theorem for 1D MLPs. This is a valid but fairly straightforward application of existing tools.

- For TT/Tucker versions, the expressivity argument is essentially the same: these are just richer multilinear combinations of univariate continuous functions. Again, density follows by the same kind of algebra‑closure and point‑separation arguments.

- Prior work already provides a D=2 version (Cho et al., 2023) and a class of separable operator networks (Yu et al., 2024). The paper asserts its approach is “simpler” and “more general”, but does not clearly articulate any fundamentally new phenomenon (e.g., explicit rank bounds, rates, or structural constraints on separability) beyond “SepNNs are universal”.

As a result, this part of the paper reads more as filling in a standard approximation result for variants of already-studied separable architectures than as a central, high‑impact theoretical advance. This matters for overall evaluation: if the NTK and preconditioning theory are not fully convincing (Issue 1–2), the universal approximation theorem alone is not strong enough to carry the paper.

## Section-by-Section Notes

### Introduction

- The problem motivation and overview of SepNNs are clear and well grounded in applications (INRs, PINNs, NeRF‑like models).

- However, the introduction repeatedly frames the contributions as rigorous and broad:
  - “provably adjusting its NTK spectrum”
  - “spectral bias characterization & alleviation”
  - “unified and broadly applicable” proofs

  These are not fully supported by the later sections. The paper should substantially down‑scope these claims, in particular regarding spectral-bias alleviation and NTK‑based convergence theory for practical (fixed‑rank) SepNNs.

### Section 2 – Approximation Theory

- The function class \(\mathcal A\) and its density in \(C(\mathcal X)\) via Stone–Weierstrass is standard. The extension to vector‑valued MLP approximations is reasonable and technically sound, though details are deferred to the appendix.

- One potential subtlety not discussed: the role of rank \(R\) in approximation quality. The theorem is purely existential; there is no discussion of how \(R\) may have to scale with approximation accuracy \(\varepsilon\) or with dimension \(D\). This is acceptable for a first‑order universal approximation theorem, but undermines any claims about practical representational efficiency of low‑rank SepNNs.

- The relation to Kolmogorov–Arnold networks (KANs) is only suggestive; nothing is actually proved or specialized for KAN-like architectures, yet the text hints at broader applicability.

Overall, sound but incremental.

### Section 3 – NTK Regimes and Spectral Bias

- **Lemma 1** (NTK formula) is a reasonable and useful decomposition. However:
  - The normalization \(1/\sqrt{R}\) in the CP architecture is introduced without discussion in Section 1; the change in Section 3 may confuse readers. More importantly, the scaling is critical for NTK limits, so it should be more centrally justified.

- **Theorem 2**:
  - The limit kernel expression \(\sum_d k(x_d,x_d')\prod_{d'\neq d} c_{d'}(x_{d'},x_{d'}')\) is plausible and consistent with law‑of‑large‑numbers behavior across latent dimensions.  
  - However, the result is proved only for two-layer factor MLPs and then declared “straightforward” to extend to deep networks. With deeper networks, the NTK recursion is more complicated and depends on layerwise scalings; the extension is not entirely trivial. Given that the paper’s main empirical architectures are not constrained to shallow networks, this is a nontrivial omission.

- **Remark 2 (NTK stays fixed)**:
  - The key assertion—“easy to show that the deterministic NTK … stays fixed during training when \(W,R\to\infty\)”—is stated but not proved in the main text. Given that for finite rank this is false (Corollary 1 introduces randomness), and that the practical regime is finite \(R\), the real applicability of a “frozen NTK” analysis is unclear.

- **Spectral bias discussion**:
  - The derivation of equation (5) is entirely standard NTK lore and correct under a fixed positive‑semidefinite kernel.  
  - The paper then jumps from this to qualitative conclusions about SepNNs’ spectral bias and sets the stage for SepPGD. However, there is no quantitative examination of the eigenvalue decay of the derived NTK in any concrete setting, beyond one illustrative numerical example (Fig. 1(d)).

- **Corollary 1 (Random NTK)**:
  - Mathematically, the convergence‑in‑distribution claim is reasonable, relying on Gaussian process limits for the factor outputs and the CP structure.  
  - The paper then concedes that, in this regime, “training dynamic can not be characterized uniformly using a fixed NTK matrix as in (5)” and leaves substantive analysis to future work. This sits uneasily with later practical claims about controlling spectral bias in exactly this regime.

### Section 4 – Separable Preconditioned Gradient Descent (SepPGD)

This section is where most of the paper’s novel algorithmic content lies, and it is also where important gaps appear.

- **Setup on grids and reshaping into tensors** is standard and well aligned with separable architectures.

- **Definition of SepPGD (equations (7)–(8))**:
  - The construction of factor preconditioners \(S_d\) from factor NTKs via eigenvalue modulation follows closely Geifman et al. / Shi et al.  
  - The definition of \(M_d\) is hard to parse in the parsed text, but the intent is clear: reweight factor outputs according to per‑dimension preconditioning and residual structure.  

- **Complexity analysis (Remark 4 and Table 1)**:
  - The asymptotic reductions—from \(O(n^D)\) matrix‑vector operations with an \(n^D \times n^D\) preconditioner to \(O(D n^2)\)-level operations with \(D\) separate \(n\times n\) preconditioners—are correct and clearly advantageous for large \(D\) and \(n\) when grid structure is present.
  - However, this comparison assumes that the competing methods truly operate on the full \(n^D \times n^D\) NTK; in practice, they often work with approximations or mini-batches (as the authors note). The narrative could better contextualize when the theoretical speedup translates into practical gains relative to sophisticated NTK approximations.

- **Lemma 2 (equivalence to large NTK-PGD in D=2)**:
  - This is an important bridge. It shows that, for the bivariate CP case on grids, SepPGD is algebraically equivalent to using a certain Kronecker‑structured preconditioner \( \tilde S\) at the full-NTK level. This is a real and nontrivial insight.
  - But this result is **restricted to D=2** in the main text; extension to D>2 is claimed to be “believed” possible but not formulated or proved. Given that most claimed applications are D≥3 (e.g., 3D PDEs, volumetric surfaces), this is a substantial gap in the formal story.

- **Spectrum improvement claim**:
  - The argument that \(K \tilde S\) has a “better” spectrum than \(K\) is only gestured at; no theorem, no condition-number bound, and no proof sketch beyond generic statements about Kronecker products.  
  - The paper then states “Therefore, the proposed SepPGD could provably and efficiently adjust the spectrum …” This is an overstatement; as written, there is no rigorous proof that the condition number is improved or that convergence rates are uniformly accelerated.

- **Non-grid inputs**:
  - The extension to non-grid inputs via Einstein summation is explained at a high level and used only in supplementary experiments. No theoretical result (like Lemma 2) is re‑established in that setting; the equivalence to a full‑NTK PGD is asserted but not carefully proved.

Overall, the algorithm is interesting and leveraging separability is a strong idea, but the formal claims about its spectral and convergence properties are not fully substantiated beyond D=2 and even there are only partially argued.

### Section 5 – Experiments

- The experimental suite is broad: KRR, images, 3D surfaces, and PDEs with PINNs, all in regimes where separable structures make sense.

- The **main qualitative finding**—SepPGD speeds up convergence (measured vs. wall-clock time) and helps capture high‑frequency details—is credible and well illustrated. This strongly supports the claim that SepPGD is *useful*.

- However, several evaluation gaps matter for a paper whose selling point is precise spectral control:

  - No **direct comparison of NTK eigenvalue spectra** before and after applying factor preconditioners (or the induced global preconditioner), even in small synthetic setups where the full NTK can be computed. Given how central “spectrum adjustment” is, this is a serious omission.

  - Absence of **ablation** comparing:
    - SepNN + vanilla GD
    - SepNN + naive per-factor learning‑rate scaling (or simple diagonal preconditioning)
    - SepNN + SepPGD  
    This would help distinguish spectral effects from simpler tuning.

  - The **MSK baseline** is only compared in the KRR setting, and even there, it is not completely clear whether hyperparameter tuning for MSK (e.g., choice of \(k\), kernel parameters) is on par with SepPGD’s tuning.

  - No statistical robustness (variances over random seeds) is reported. Given that Corollary 1 emphasizes randomness in NTKs at fixed rank, point estimates are not fully persuasive.

Collectively, the experiments convincingly show that SepPGD can be helpful, but they do not substantively validate the **mechanism** claimed (spectrum manipulation / spectral-bias alleviation via NTKs) nor tightly match the regimes analyzed in Section 3.

### Conclusions and Discussion

- The discussion reiterates strong claims about “theoretical approximation ability, training behavior (e.g., NTK regime), and addressing … optimization challenge” without acknowledging the limitations of the NTK analysis at fixed rank and the incomplete status of the spectral-bias proof.

- There is no explicit limitations section; in particular, the gap between theory (infinite width & rank, D=2 equivalence) and practice (finite, often small rank; D≥3; random NTKs) is not candidly discussed.

## Strengths

- Clear, coherent **formalization of SepNN architectures** (CP, TT, Tucker) and their relation to tensor decompositions and INRs/PINNs. This helps unify a scattered literature.

- A **clean universal approximation theorem** for multivariate separable architectures (CP/TT/Tucker) using a standard but well-structured Stone–Weierstrass + universal approximation argument, extending earlier D=2 and sine-specific results.

- A **useful NTK decomposition (Lemma 1)** and distinct asymptotic regimes (Theorem 2, Corollary 1), clarifying how width and rank interact in SepNNs’ kernel limits.

- The **SepPGD algorithm** is a clever application of separability: it decomposes a prohibitive NTK-based preconditioner into per-dimension factors, leading to substantial asymptotic complexity reductions on grids. The bivariate equivalence (Lemma 2) to a Kronecker-structured NTK preconditioner is a nontrivial and appealing insight.

- **Empirical results** are broad and consistent: across KRR, INRs, and PINNs, SepPGD reliably accelerates training and often improves high-frequency reconstruction, which is exactly what one expects from mitigating spectral bias.

## Overall Assessment

The paper makes several interesting and partially novel contributions: it systematizes separable neural architectures, provides a sound universal approximation theorem, characterizes NTK regimes in certain asymptotics, and proposes a separable preconditioned GD that is both elegant and empirically effective. However, the central theoretical claim—that SepPGD *provably* adjusts the NTK spectrum to alleviate spectral bias for practical SepNNs—is not actually established: the deterministic NTK analysis applies only in an infinite‑rank limit that conflicts with the intended low‑rank regime; the random‑NTK regime is acknowledged but left unanalyzed; and the spectrum‑improvement argument is at best heuristic even in the D=2 case, with no extension beyond hand‑waving to D>2. Given the weight placed on this claim in the abstract and framing, this is more than a minor gap: it means the core theoretical contribution on optimization and spectral bias does not stand as advertised. The universal approximation result and the empirical success of SepPGD are not, in my view, strong enough on their own to justify acceptance at a top venue without a more honest and rigorous treatment of these theoretical limitations. I would not recommend acceptance in the current form; the paper would need to (i) substantially strengthen the NTK/spectrum analysis or (ii) scale back its theoretical claims and reframe SepPGD primarily as a practical, empirically validated heuristic.
### Neutral Reviewer
## Balanced Review

### Summary
This paper provides three theoretical contributions for Separable Neural Networks (SepNNs): (1) a universal approximation theorem proving SepNNs with CP, TT, or Tucker decompositions can approximate any continuous multivariate function on compact sets, (2) an NTK regime characterization showing the SepNN NTK converges to a deterministic kernel under infinite width and rank, and to a random kernel under infinite width but fixed rank, and (3) an efficient Separable Preconditioned Gradient Descent (SepPGD) method that exploits the separable structure to achieve O(nD) complexity for n^D grid samples, provably adjusting the NTK spectrum to alleviate spectral bias.

### Strengths
1. **Unified approximation theory**: The proof technique combining Stone-Weierstrass with the universal approximation theorem provides a clean, unified framework applicable to CP, TT, and Tucker SepNN formulations (Theorem 1), subsuming prior bivariate results (Cho et al., 2023) as a special case and generalizing beyond specific activation functions (Yu et al., 2024).

2. **Practically relevant NTK distinction**: The distinction between deterministic NTK (infinite rank) and random NTK (fixed rank) in Corollary 1 is valuable because practical SepNNs typically use small ranks for efficiency and generalization. The empirical validation in Fig. 1(a-c) clearly confirms these distinct regimes.

3. **Significant computational gains in SepPGD**: The reduction from O(n^D) to O(nD) in preconditioner application (Table 1) is substantial. Lemma 2 provides a formal equivalence between SepPGD and classical NTK-based PGD via Kronecker products for D=2, giving theoretical grounding for the method.

4. **Comprehensive empirical evaluation**: Experiments span kernel ridge regression, image representation, surface representation, and PINNs (Figs. 2–4), consistently demonstrating that SepPGD accelerates convergence of SepNNs without harming generalization, including in noisy settings.

5. **Elegant NTK decomposition**: Lemma 1 showing the SepNN NTK decomposes as a weighted sum of factor NTKs is clean and enables the subsequent analysis and efficient preconditioning.

### Weaknesses
1. **Limited novelty in approximation theorem**: While the result is important, it is essentially a straightforward application of Stone-Weierstrass to the class of separable functions followed by the standard universal approximation theorem. The separable function class A satisfying Stone-Weierstrass conditions is relatively expected, reducing the technical surprise of the contribution.

2. **Incomplete extension to D>2 for SepPGD equivalence**: Lemma 2 proving equivalence between SepPGD and classical PGD is restricted to D=2. The paper states this "can be readily extended to multivariate cases D>2" (Section 4), but no proof or formal statement is provided, leaving a gap in the theoretical foundation for the most general setting.

3. **Informal convergence analysis for SepPGD**: The argument that SepPGD improves the NTK spectrum after Lemma 2 is heuristic rather than rigorous. The reasoning about Kronecker product eigenvalues improving the condition number of KŠ̃ is sketched informally ("This can possibly be verified"), and no formal convergence rate bound or guarantee is established for the proposed method.

4. **Limited practical guidance on rank selection**: The theory shows infinite rank yields deterministic NTK while fixed rank yields random NTK, but there is no analysis or empirical study guiding the practical trade-off between rank R (affecting both representation capacity and NTK determinism) and computational cost.

5. **Grid-input restriction for SepPGD efficiency**: The O(nD) complexity of SepPGD relies fundamentally on grid-structured inputs. The brief discussion of non-grid inputs in Section 4 is underdeveloped and not empirically evaluated, limiting the applicability scope of the main algorithmic contribution.

### Novelty & Significance
The paper provides a systematic theoretical treatment of SepNNs that was previously lacking. The universal approximation theorem, while not technically surprising, formally establishes representation completeness that practitioners implicitly assumed. The NTK analysis is a natural but valuable extension of standard NTK theory to the separable structure, with the fixed-rank random NTK result being the more novel and practically relevant finding. The SepPGD method is the most significant practical contribution, achieving substantial efficiency gains through structural exploitation. However, the theoretical analysis of SepPGD's convergence properties is underdeveloped. Overall, the work fills an important gap in understanding SepNNs and provides useful algorithmic tools, though individual components vary in depth and novelty.

### Suggestions for Improvement
1. **Provide a formal theorem and proof for SepPGD equivalence when D>2**, extending Lemma 2 to the general multivariate case, which is the primary setting of interest for SepNNs.

2. **Establish a rigorous convergence rate analysis for SepPGD**, e.g., bounding the condition number improvement of the preconditioned system and providing convergence rate guarantees, rather than relying on the informal Kronecker product argument.

3. **Include an empirical or theoretical study on the effect of rank R** on the NTK randomness, spectral bias severity, and the effectiveness of SepPGD, which would bridge the theory-practice gap and provide actionable guidance.

4. **Evaluate SepPGD on non-grid inputs** more thoroughly, since many practical PINN and INR scenarios involve irregularly sampled data. Even limited experiments would clarify the method's practical scope.

5. **Compare against a broader set of baselines** for spectral bias mitigation (e.g., Fourier feature mappings, activation function modifications) rather than primarily NTK-based preconditioning methods, to better contextualize the contribution.
### Spark
## How to Improve This Paper

### Missing Experiments (top 3-5 only)
1. **No comparison with standard optimizers (e.g., Adam, SGD with momentum).** SepPGD is only compared against other NTK-based PGD methods, but in practice SepNNs are trained with Adam. Without this baseline, it is unclear whether SepPGD's benefits over standard training are meaningful or whether simpler optimizer tweaks could achieve similar gains.

2. **No experiments on multivariate cases (D > 2) for SepPGD.** The paper's title and motivation emphasize general multivariate functions, yet all major experiments (image representation, KRR) are D = 2. The D = 3 surface experiment and PINN experiments show limited evidence. Without systematic higher-dimensional evaluation, the claimed generality of SepPGD is unsubstantiated.

3. **No ablation on rank R vs. SepPGD effectiveness.** The NTK theory requires infinite rank for deterministic kernel behavior, but practice uses small R. The paper lacks experiments showing how SepPGD performance varies with R, which is critical since the random NTK regime (Corollary 1) raises questions about preconditioner reliability at low rank.

4. **No evaluation of SepPGD on non-grid inputs in the main paper.** The efficiency claims rely heavily on grid structure, and the paper briefly mentions non-grid applicability in an appendix. Experiments are needed to validate whether SepPGD remains effective when the Kronecker structure assumption is violated.

### Deeper Analysis Needed (top 3-5 only)
1. **Lemma 2 (equivalence of SepPGD and classical PGD) is only proven for D = 2.** The extension to D > 2 is stated as "believed" but not proven. This is the theoretical backbone justifying SepPGD's effectiveness, and without it, the core claim that SepPGD provably adjusts the NTK spectrum for general SepNNs lacks rigor.

2. **Theorem 1 provides no quantitative approximation bounds.** The universal approximation result is purely existential — no bound on required rank R or width W for a given error ε is provided. This limits the theorem's practical value, as it cannot guide architecture choices or explain the approximation hardness of different function classes.

3. **The spectral bias alleviation claim lacks a formal convergence rate guarantee for SepPGD.** The paper argues heuristically that S̃ improves the spectrum of KS̃, but no theorem proves that the condition number of KS̃ is bounded or that convergence accelerates by a guaranteed factor. The connection between the Kronecker-structured preconditioner and actual eigenvalue improvement is informal.

4. **No analysis of the gap between the pseudo-NTK K̃ = KΘ₁⊗I+I⊗KΘ₂ and the true NTK K.** The preconditioner S̃ is constructed from K̃ rather than K, and Lemma 2 shows equivalence only under K̃. The error between K̃ and K — and its impact on convergence — is not analyzed, leaving open whether SepPGD truly targets the correct NTK spectrum.

### Visualizations & Case Studies
1. **No visualization of NTK eigenvalue spectra before/after SepPGD for the actual training problem.** The paper shows NTK spectrum in Fig. 1(d) for characterization, but never visualizes the effective spectrum of KS̃ vs. K to directly confirm that SepPGD actually flattens the spectrum as claimed.

2. **No failure case analysis.** Showing where SepPGD fails or underperforms — e.g., when rank is very small, when data is non-grid, or when the target function is not well-approximated by low-rank separable structure — would reveal the method's boundaries and strengthen credibility.

### Obvious Next Steps
1. **Prove the D > 2 generalization of Lemma 2.** This is the single most important missing piece — without it, SepPGD's theoretical justification for the general multivariate case is incomplete, which directly undermines the paper's core contribution.

2. **Compare SepPGD against Adam and other standard optimizers** on all tasks, reporting wall-clock time and iteration convergence. This is needed to establish practical relevance beyond the narrow comparison with other PGD methods.

3. **Provide explicit approximation error bounds** (rank/width vs. ε) for Theorem 1, at minimum for specific function classes (e.g., Lipschitz functions), so the approximation theory has quantitative teeth rather than being purely existential.

### Other stuff you can add
1. **Discuss computational overhead of preconditioner updates.** The paper mentions updating preconditioners every 10 iterations but does not report the wall-clock overhead of constructing {S_d} relative to forward/backward passes, which matters for the claimed efficiency advantage.
2. **Clarify the relationship between SepPGD and second-order methods** (e.g., Gauss-Newton, Kronecker-factored approximate curvature) since the Kronecker structure of the preconditioner resembles K-FAC-style approximations; situating SepPGD within this literature would strengthen motivation.
### Human Finder
Now I have gathered sufficient relevant reviews. Let me synthesize the findings into a structured review.

**Strengths:**

1. The paper provides a unified theoretical framework for SepNNs, establishing universal approximation (Theorem 1), NTK regimes (Theorem 2, Corollary 1), and a practical optimization method (SepPGD). The combination of Weierstrass-based approximation and universal approximation theory for the approximation result is elegant and the proof technique is cleaner than prior work (Cho et al., 2023).

2. The derivation of NTK regimes under both infinite-width/infinite-rank (deterministic kernel) and infinite-width/fixed-rank (random kernel) conditions provides valuable dual insights into SepNN training dynamics, particularly the insight that infinite rank is necessary for a deterministic NTK.

3. The SepPGD method achieving O(nD) complexity for n^D training samples is a significant practical improvement over prior NTK-based preconditioning methods (Geifman et al., 2024) that scale as O(n^D), and the Kronecker product structure enabling this efficiency is well-motivated.

4. Extensive experiments across KRR, image/surface representation (INRs), and PINNs demonstrate the broad applicability and effectiveness of SepPGD for alleviating spectral bias.

**Weaknesses:**

1. **The NTK theoretical results rely on strong infinite-width assumptions that may limit practical relevance.** The deterministic NTK result (Theorem 2) requires both width W→∞ and rank R→∞, and even the fixed-rank result (Corollary 1) requires W→∞. In practice, SepNNs use finite width and often small rank to promote low-dimensional representations. As noted in reviews of similar NTK-based papers: "it is not clear how much things will break down when we look at a finite-width NN" (pv2U1BeC5Z), and "the theory in this work fails to extend to...the changing NTK regime" where "the NTK changes significantly in most interesting cases" (ogxrdvFdx5). The paper acknowledges this for the random NTK case (Remark 3), noting that training dynamics "can not be characterized uniformly using a fixed NTK matrix," but the empirical evaluation does not systematically test how well the theoretical predictions hold when the width/rank are modest (e.g., how sensitive SepPGD's effectiveness is to network width and rank choices).

2. **The relationship and incremental contribution over Geifman et al. (2024) needs clearer articulation.** The core idea of modifying gradient descent using a matrix derived from the NTK spectrum originated from Geifman et al. (2024), and SepPGD's primary contribution is making this efficient for SepNNs via separability. However, as stressed in reviews of similar preconditioning papers: "A significant part of the methodological contribution...overlaps what was proposed by Geifman et al. (2024). A clearer positioning of the contribution relative to this paper is needed" (TNYLCF7vZA, Reviewer 4). While Lemma 2 establishes the equivalence between SepPGD and NTK-based PGD for the bivariate case, the extension to D>2 is stated as "believed" to be "readily" extendable without proof. This leaves the theoretical grounding for the key practical setting (multivariate SepNNs) incomplete.

3. **The SepPGD's effectiveness on noisy data and generalization is underexplored.** As raised in reviews of related spectral bias work: "In some cases, this spectral bias can be seen as beneficial, as it can reduce the noise that is often present in the high frequencies of the data... How would the results change if the data was noisy?" (TNYLCF7vZA, Reviewer 4). The paper's experiments primarily test noiseless or low-noise settings (e.g., noise standard deviation 0.01 for KRR). Since alleviating spectral bias accelerates learning of high-frequency components, it may also amplify noise, and this trade-off deserves more systematic investigation.

4. **The hyperparameter k in the modulation function g(λ_i) lacks principled selection guidance and ablation.** The modulation function sets g(λ_i) = λ^k for the first k eigenvalues, but the strategy for choosing k is not discussed, and corresponding ablation studies are missing. As noted in a review of a similarly structured preconditioning method: "The effectiveness of the proposed method depends on the pre-selection of the hyperparameters...the strategy of hyperparameter choosing is not discussed, and the corresponding ablation studies are missing" (TNYLCF7vZA, Reviewer 1). The paper reports that the preconditioner is "efficiently updated every ten iterations" but does not analyze sensitivity to this update frequency or to the choice of k across different tasks.

5. **Experimental comparison with more recent and diverse baselines is limited.** For INR tasks, comparisons are primarily against MSK (Geifman et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025), but do not include alternative spectral bias mitigation methods such as Fourier feature reparameterization variants or other activation design approaches. For PINNs, only the separable PINN (Cho et al., 2023) is tested. As noted in reviews of similar INR papers: "comparison with the latest methods such as WIRE, and Gaussian-based INRs are missing. Without proper comparisons with those latest methods, one cannot see the significance of the proposed method" (NrLXQWwCMg, Reviewer 2). Additionally, the PINN experiments use only grid samples, which aligns with SepPGD's efficiency advantage, but non-grid scenarios (common in practice) are barely tested (deferred to a brief appendix mention).

--- Merged Review ---
## Summary

The paper studies separable neural networks (SepNNs) that represent multivariate functions via linear combinations of univariate neural factors (CP, TT, Tucker forms). It proves a universal approximation theorem for such architectures, analyzes their neural tangent kernel (NTK) limits under different width–rank asymptotics, and proposes Separable Preconditioned Gradient Descent (SepPGD), an NTK-inspired preconditioner that exploits separability to reduce computational cost and empirically alleviate spectral bias on grids in INRs and PINNs.

## Strengths

- **Clear formalization of SepNN architectures.**  
  The paper gives a coherent, tensor-decomposition–based description of CP, TT, and Tucker SepNNs ((2)–(3)), and explains the computational savings on grid inputs (O(nD) vs. O(n^D)), which directly underpins the algorithmic contribution.

- **Sound and unified universal approximation result.**  
  Theorem 1 establishes that CP, TT, and Tucker SepNNs with univariate MLP factors and non-polynomial activations are universal approximators on compact product domains. The argument—Stone–Weierstrass density of separable functions, plus vector-valued universal approximation—is technically standard but correctly executed and genuinely unifies/extends prior D=2 and special-activation results.

- **Useful NTK formulation and asymptotic regimes.**  
  Lemma 1 expresses the CP SepNN NTK as a sum over factor NTKs with multiplicative weights, which is both transparent and practically useful. Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 cleanly distinguish two regimes: deterministic NTK for width W→∞ and rank R→∞, and random NTK for width→∞ with fixed rank. The empirical checks in Fig. 1(a–c) substantiate these asymptotic claims at a qualitative level.

- **Conceptually appealing and efficient SepPGD.**  
  Section 4 leverages separability to build per-dimension preconditioners {S_d} from factor NTKs and defines SepPGD updates that operate on factor networks rather than the full SepNN. Lemma 2 (for D=2) rigorously connects SepPGD to classical NTK-based PGD with a Kronecker-structured preconditioner \(\tilde S = S_1\otimes I + I\otimes S_2\). The complexity analysis (Remark 4, Table 1) shows clear asymptotic gains: applying preconditioning scales as O(nD) using D n×n matrices instead of O(n^D) with an n^D×n^D matrix.

- **Broad, well-aligned empirical evaluation.**  
  Experiments cover kernel ridge regression (KRR), 2D image INRs, 3D surface INRs, and 3D PDEs via separable PINNs. Across these, SepPGD consistently accelerates convergence in wall-clock time, and visual results show better recovery of high-frequency details and PDE solutions at comparable iteration counts.

## Weaknesses

### Fatal

None. The paper is a real paper with nontrivial and mostly correct content; the main issues are overclaiming and incompleteness rather than fundamental invalidity.

### Major

- **Overstated “provable” spectral-bias alleviation and incomplete spectrum analysis.**  
  The abstract and body claim that SepPGD “provably adjusts the eigenvalue distribution of [the] NTK matrix, effectively alleviating spectral bias” and is used to argue about convergence improvements. However:
  - Lemma 2 only proves that, for D=2 on grids and under a specific construction of S_d, SepPGD’s parameter update equals a full-NTK PGD update with a structured preconditioner \(\tilde S\).  
  - The key spectral claim—that KS̃ has strictly or quantifiably better eigenvalue distribution (e.g., smaller condition number, faster convergence) than K—is not proved. The text explicitly says “This can possibly be verified” and then gives an informal argument about eigenvalues of Kronecker products and S_d having “better spectrum” than K_{Θ_d}. There is no theorem, no bound, and no precise condition under which the global NTK K is close to the surrogate \(\tilde K = K_{\Theta_1}\otimes I + I\otimes K_{\Theta_2}\).  
  - For D>2, the extension of Lemma 2 and the convergence/spectrum analysis are left to “future research”.  
  Given the weight placed on “provably adjusting its NTK spectrum” in the framing, the current theory does not substantiate that core optimization claim beyond a limited algebraic equivalence in the bivariate case.

- **Mismatch between NTK theory and the practically relevant fixed–small-rank regime.**  
  The deterministic NTK analysis (Theorem 2, Remark 2, equation (5)) assumes both W→∞ and R→∞, i.e., very large rank. Yet the paper explicitly motivates SepNNs by their use of small ranks for efficiency and generalization, and Corollary 1 shows that at fixed R the NTK is random and the training dynamics cannot be captured by a fixed kernel. Despite this:
  - The spectral-bias discussion and convergence analysis rely entirely on the fixed-NTK ODE (5) and eigen-decomposition K = ∑ λ_i v_i v_i^⊤.  
  - There is no attempt to justify using the deterministic NTK picture as an approximation for the finite-width, finite, often small-rank networks used in experiments, nor to connect to the random-NTK regime in Corollary 1 via stochastic analysis.  
  As a result, the “NTK regimes and spectral bias characterization” contribution is rigorous only in an asymptotic regime that conflicts with the main intended usage (low-rank SepNNs), and its relevance to the empirically studied setting remains largely heuristic.

- **SepPGD theory for general D is not worked out.**  
  The D=2 equivalence in Lemma 2 is nontrivial and valuable, but the paper’s promises and experiments are for multivariate SepNNs (D≥3 for volumetric occupancy and 3D PDEs). For D>2:
  - The paper only asserts that Lemma 2 “can be readily extended” but does not provide a statement or proof.  
  - The definition of M_d in (7)–(8) for general D is hard to parse in the extracted text and not backed by a global NTK-level equivalence like in Lemma 2.  
  - In non-grid settings, the extension via an Einstein-product construction is described informally; no theorem shows equivalence to a full-NTK PGD or quantifies the approximation.  
  This leaves a significant gap between the nicely proved D=2 case and the general multivariate setting that motivates the paper’s title and many experiments.

- **Universal approximation result is mainly existential and of modest standalone impact.**  
  Theorem 1 is mathematically sound but:
  - It is essentially a fairly direct application of Stone–Weierstrass to separable continuous functions on product domains, plus standard vector-valued universal approximation. The function class \(\mathcal A\) in Section 2 is a natural separable algebra, and checking the Stone–Weierstrass conditions is routine.  
  - There is no quantitative control over rank R or ranks (R_1,…,R_{D-1}) as a function of error ε and dimension D. Thus the theorem does not inform when low-rank separable models suffice or how rank must grow with approximation difficulty, which would be especially relevant in a paper that also emphasizes efficiency and low-rank structure.  
  Absent stronger NTK/optimization theory, this approximation result, while nice, is not by itself a high-impact contribution.

### Minor

- **Lack of empirical evidence directly connecting SepPGD to NTK spectrum changes.**  
  The stated mechanism is spectral: preconditioning should flatten or otherwise improve the NTK eigenvalue spectrum. The paper does show initial NTK eigenvalue decay for an unpreconditioned SepNN (Fig. 1(d)), but it does not:
  - Visualize eigenvalues of the effective preconditioned kernel (e.g., KS̃) vs. K, even on small synthetic problems where full NTKs are tractable.  
  - Correlate measured spectral changes with convergence acceleration.  
  This weakens the paper’s mechanistic story; we see that SepPGD helps empirically, but not that it helps *via* the NTK spectral adjustments it is designed to approximate.

- **Sensitivity to hyperparameters in SepPGD is not explored.**  
  The construction of S_d uses a modulation function g(λ_i) that sets g(λ_i)=λ_k for i≤k and g(λ_i)=λ_i otherwise, and factor preconditioners are updated every ten iterations. The paper does not:
  - Explain how k is chosen across tasks or how sensitive performance is to k.  
  - Ablate the preconditioner update frequency.  
  Without at least brief sensitivity analyses, it is hard to assess robustness and ease of use.

- **Baseline coverage is somewhat narrow.**  
  For KRR, the comparison includes classical NTK-based PGD and MSK (Geifman et al., 2024). For image/surface representation and PINNs, the baselines are mainly SepNN with vanilla training and MSK. There is no comparison to:
  - Standard optimizers like Adam or SGD with momentum on SepNNs, which most practitioners would use.  
  - Alternative spectral-bias mitigation strategies (e.g., Fourier features, other architectural tricks) in INR or PINN contexts.  
  This limits the ability to judge how competitive SepPGD is against strong but non-NTK baselines.

- **Fixed-vs-noisy data behavior is only lightly touched.**  
  The KRR experiments include both noiseless and small-noise (std 0.01) cases, but broader questions about whether accelerating high-frequency learning might amplify noise are not explored. For tasks like PDEs or natural images, some discussion or empirical check of robustness in noisier settings would be valuable.

- **Clarity/notation issues around the main algorithm.**  
  In the extracted text, equations (7)–(8) are difficult to parse; even allowing for PDF-to-text artifacts, several key constructs (outer product over d≠d, the exact dimensions of M_d, and the role of LR_r=1 concatenation) are nontrivial to decode from the main body. Given that this is the central algorithm, a clearer, more self-contained presentation in the main text would improve accessibility.

### Trivial

- Minor consistency issues, such as the change from the original CP SepNN form in (2) to the normalized form with 1/√R in Section 3, are not explicitly motivated in the main text and may confuse some readers, though they are standard in NTK derivations.

## Nice-to-Haves

- A small-scale synthetic example where the full NTK of a low-dimensional SepNN can be computed exactly, showing:
  - eigenvalue spectra of K vs. the approximate preconditioned kernel KS̃, and  
  - matching convergence trajectories between SepPGD and the equivalent full-NTK PGD.  
  This would concretely validate both the spectrum-improvement story and Lemma 2-style equivalence.

- Some quantitative discussion or toy analysis of how rank R influences approximation quality vs. NTK randomness, perhaps for simple separable target functions, to begin bridging the approximation theory and NTK regimes.

- A limitations section explicitly acknowledging that the deterministic NTK theory is asymptotic and that the current spectral-bias theory does not rigorously extend to the small-rank, finite-width, D>2 regimes actually used in experiments.

## Removed Points

These points are flagged to be removed, treat them with caution:

- **Claim that SepPGD is not evaluated on multivariate (D>2) cases.**  
  The harsh critic suggested that “all major experiments” are D=2, but the paper explicitly reports 3D surface representation (volumetric occupancy grids) and 3D PDEs (diffusion, Klein–Gordon, Helmholtz) using separable PINNs with D=3. These are genuine multivariate cases; while the theory for D>2 is incomplete, the experiments are not purely bivariate.

- **Criticism that the NTK regime analysis is “unrealistic” per se.**  
  While it is true that W→∞, R→∞ are asymptotic limits, this is standard in NTK theory and the paper itself clearly highlights the difference between infinite and fixed rank, including Corollary 1 and Remark 3. The valid concern is about the *connection* to finite, small-rank practice (kept above), not about using asymptotics at all.

- **Assertion that SepPGD is only tested in noiseless scenarios.**  
  The paper explicitly states that KRR experiments follow Geifman et al. (2024) with both noisy and noiseless cases and reports robustness in the noisy regime (“In the presence of noise, SepPGD remains robust”). The degree of exploration is limited, but noise is not entirely ignored.

## Novel Insights

The most valuable novel insight is that, for separable CP architectures, one can decompose the NTK and the associated NTK-based preconditioning in a way that admits a Kronecker structure at the full-network level and factorized preconditioners at the implementation level. Lemma 2 shows that for D=2 on grids, an apparently cheaper, factor-wise update is exactly equivalent to a specific Kronecker-structured preconditioned NTK step. This insight highlights a general design pattern: separable factorization in function space can translate to separable structure in the NTK and its preconditioners, which in turn can yield substantial algorithmic savings without altering the underlying kernel method—at least in low-D, grid-structured settings.

## Suggestions

- **Tone down or precisely qualify spectral-bias and “provable spectrum adjustment” claims.**  
  Rephrase statements in the abstract/introduction and Section 4 to reflect what is actually proved:  
  - rigorously: existence and form of NTK regimes; algebraic equivalence of SepPGD to a certain NTK-PGD in D=2;  
  - heuristically/empirically: that SepPGD appears to alleviate spectral bias and accelerate convergence in practice.

- **Add a formal theorem for D>2 SepPGD, or else explicitly limit claims to D=2.**  
  Ideally, extend Lemma 2 to general D, stating the exact Kronecker-structured preconditioner and proving parameter-update equivalence under clear assumptions. If this is technically challenging, at least be explicit that the current theoretical equivalence is proved only in the bivariate case, and adjust the main claims accordingly.

- **Provide at least qualitative spectral evidence for SepPGD’s mechanism.**  
  On a small problem where computing full NTKs is feasible:
  - show the eigenvalue spectra of K vs. the effective preconditioned operator (or KS̃) before/after constructing S_d, and  
  - align these with observed convergence rates.  
  This would significantly strengthen the spectral-bias narrative.

- **Clarify how SepPGD compares to standard optimizers.**  
  Add baselines using Adam or SGD with momentum for SepNNs on at least some INR and PINN tasks, comparing both convergence speed (time-to-error) and final quality. This will better position SepPGD as either a practically compelling method or primarily a theoretically motivated tool.

- **Include basic hyperparameter sensitivity/ablation.**  
  For one or two representative tasks, vary:
  - k in the modulation function g(λ_i), and  
  - the frequency of preconditioner recomputation,  
  and report performance. Even coarse-grained results will give readers a sense of robustness and tuning burden.

- **Improve the presentation of SepPGD in the main text.**  
  Rewrite the definition of M_d and the update rule in clearer linear-algebra notation (possibly with a simple worked example for D=2 or D=3) so that readers can understand the algorithm without relying on the appendix or deciphering Einstein summation conventions.

### Evaluation on Standard Axes

- **Originality:** Moderate. The approximation and NTK analyses are natural extensions of existing theory to separable architectures. SepPGD’s main originality lies in exploiting separability to factor NTK preconditioners, with a solid D=2 equivalence result.

- **Importance of question:** Reasonable. Understanding and improving training of efficient separable architectures (INRs, PINNs) is an active and relevant direction.

- **Support for claims:** Mixed. Approximation and NTK regime claims are well supported. Claims about spectral-bias alleviation and provable spectrum adjustment for general SepNNs are not fully backed by theory, though empirical evidence is encouraging.

- **Soundness of experiments:** Generally solid for showing usefulness, but lacking in comparisons to non-NTK baselines, spectral diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses.

- **Clarity:** Good overall on high-level ideas and theory; weaker around the precise specification and intuition of SepPGD in the main body.

- **Value to community:** Moderate. The paper could be quite useful if the claims and limitations are made more precise and if at least some of the suggested strengthening is implemented; in its current form it is more of a promising but somewhat oversold step than a definitive treatment.

## Score and Decision

For calibration, I compared against:

- **TNYLCF7vZA (Inductive Gradient Adjustment for Spectral Bias in INRs)** — a closely related NTK-based preconditioning work with mixed reviews (8,3,5,3) and an overall rejection, primarily due to overreliance on NTK asymptotics and incomplete justification of spectral-bias claims. The current paper is conceptually similar but somewhat more careful in distinguishing NTK regimes and provides a stronger architectural context (SepNNs, grids).

- **RFLZFxoLnE (Modify Training Direction in Function Space to Reduce Generalization Error)** — another NTK-based training-modification paper with scores around 3–5 and rejection, where limits of NTK-based theory for practical networks and insufficient experimental grounding were central concerns. The present submission is at least as strong empirically but has comparable theory–practice gaps on optimization aspects.

- **ogxrdvFdx5 (ReLU soothes NTK conditioning)** — NTK-conditioning and optimization paper (3,3,6,5, rejected) with interesting theoretical insights but limited robustness of assumptions and applicability; similar pattern of strong but narrow theory vs. practice.

Given these anchors, this paper is stronger than some purely-theoretical NTK works with minimal empirical backup, because it does include substantial experiments and a solid approximation result. However, the central optimization/spectral-bias claims are overstated relative to what is proved, and key theory for the general multivariate and fixed-rank regimes is missing.

I therefore place it in the “weak reject” range: valuable ideas and decent execution, but below the bar for a top venue without significant tightening of theory and claims.

### Harsh Critic
## Critical Issues

### 1. Central “equivalence” claim is overstated and only holds in a narrow, local, and highly conditioned sense  
**Type: Structural**  
**Where:** Abstract; Introduction (“we prove that, to first order, these techniques are *equivalent*”), Theorem 4.2, Section 5 (alignment, no-free-lunch), Section 6 (generalization).

The paper repeatedly claims that activation steering and influence functions are “equivalent,” and that “any steering vector can be represented as an influence weighting … and vice versa.” The actual theory, as visible from the fragments, is much weaker and substantially more conditional:

- At the **Jacobian level**, matching requires Im(J\_{\theta→y}) ⊆ Im(J\_{h→y}); this is encoded in the “feasibility” assumption (Section 2, Assumptions) and Theorem 5.1/5.2. This is a strong structural condition and is not generically true. When it fails, Theorem 6.2 gives only a **strict upper bound** on what steering can approximate.
- The no-free-lunch theorem (6.2) makes it explicit that when the principal-angle cosine γ(x)=ω(x) < 1, steering cannot in general replicate parameter perturbations: even infinite-norm activation changes are bounded by γ. This directly contradicts sweeping language like “any steering vector can be represented … and vice versa.”
- The first-order Taylor argument is **pointwise in x** and **infinitesimal in α and influence mass**; the equivalence is not shown to hold uniformly over inputs, nor for practically relevant, finite-magnitude interventions.

So the core formal result is:

> For a fixed x, and for an infinitesimal parameter perturbation Δθ whose induced logit change lies in the logit subspace Im(J\_{h→y}(x)), there exists a unique minimum-norm Δh (IAS) such that J\_{h→y}Δh = J\_{\theta→y}Δθ, and the relative error decreases with γ(x).

This is not the same as a global “activation steering and influence are equivalent” statement, and it certainly does not justify “any steering vector ↔ any influence weighting.” The language of the abstract and introduction overspecifies the claim relative to what the mathematics actually supports.

Because this overclaim is exactly the headline contribution and is used to motivate all downstream ideas (mapping back to causal data, “single efficient workflow,” strong practical guarantees), this is not a cosmetic issue. Theoretical results as stated (bounded approximation under alignment) are meaningful, but they do *not* validate the central equivalence narrative. In its current form, the paper sells a much stronger story than its theorems warrant.

### 2. Data-level “causal” interpretation of ρ\_s is not justified by the presented theory  
**Type: Structural / Evidential (leans structural because it’s a conceptual misuse)**  
**Where:** Section 4.1 (Corollary 1, Theorem 4.2), plus narratives: “causal corollary,” “most causal training documents,” “map undesired behaviors back to causal training examples,” Abstract and Introduction.

Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 1 establish **existence** of a signed measure ρ\_s over training points such that

- The first-order logit shift from steering is matched:  
  f\_{\theta}^{a,α}(x) − f\_{\theta}(x) = Σ\_z ρ\_s(z) I(z→x) + O(α²),
- and among all such measures, ρ\_s is ℓ₁-minimal (given affine independence of the influence vectors).

This is a **purely linear-algebraic decomposition**: find signed coefficients in the basis of influence vectors that match a desired small logit displacement, and pick the minimum-ℓ₁ solution. From this, the paper jumps to:

- “ρ\_s pinpoints the *fewest* training examples to relabel/remove/examine to reproduce the behavioral change.”
- “Implication. Given an empirical steering direction, the associated measure ρ\_s points straight to the *most causal* training documents.”
- And in the Introduction and Abstract, the claim that this yields a constructive algorithm for “mapping undesired behaviors back to causal training examples.”

Problems:

1. **Identifiability:** Nothing in the theory prevents multiple, very different measures ρ from yielding nearly identical first-order shifts (especially in overparameterized, redundant settings). Affine independence of the influence vectors is (i) extremely stringent for real networks and (ii) even if it held, it only guarantees uniqueness of the ℓ₁-minimal solution among *algebraically equivalent decompositions*. It does not align that solution with any meaningful statistical or causal notion of data “responsibility.”

2. **Causal semantics:** The definition of influence functions already gives a counterfactual notion (“if I up-weighted this point, what happens?”) but is well-known to be fragile and sensitive to modeling assumptions and Hessian approximations. Composing these with a further basis-expansion and a minimal-ℓ₁ objective and then calling the resulting ρ\_s the “most causal” set of points is a much stronger interpretive leap than standard influence-function usage. The paper does not justify that ℓ₁-minimal decompositions correspond to anything like “fewest causal points” in a causal or even approximate-counterfactual sense.

3. **No empirical sanity check:** There are no experiments showing that top-mass ρ\_s examples, when removed or relabeled, actually reproduce the steering effect in practice. Without such evidence, labeling ρ\_s as “causal” is speculative.

Given that “causal attribution back to training data” is one of the three headline payoffs in the abstract, this conceptual stretch matters. The current results support a *representer-type* statement (“any small steering displacement can be expressed as a linear combination of influence vectors”), not a validated workflow for reliably finding causal training examples.

### 3. Experimental evidence is too narrow and weak to support the claimed practical workflow and generality  
**Type: Evidential**  
**Where:** Section 7 subsections; overall claims in Introduction (“unified workflow,” “scale to billion-parameter models”), Conclusion.

The experiments are:

- Detoxification on GPT-2 Medium: compare IAS vs. CAA on toxicity (TOXIGEN) and benign perplexity (WikiText) at one layer (ϖ=8). Differences in toxicity and PPL are small; no significance or variance is reported; configuration details are sparse (exact magnitude constraints, how CAA is tuned, etc.).
- First-order equivalence check: plot predicted vs. actual logit shifts, reporting cosine 0.978 and slope 1.50 for 5000 prompt–token pairs at one layer. This supports that *some* first-order approximation holds locally, but the slope ≠ 1 already reveals systematic bias; there is no breakdown by prompt class, token type, or magnitude of Δ, and no analysis of where approximation fails.
- Alignment vs. depth on GPT-2: ω rises from ~0.64 to ~0.94 with depth. This is interesting but only on a single model/dataset combination.
- Spectral optimality on ResNet-50 for the “horse” class: they estimate the leading direction and compare it to random directions; the spectral direction lies in the tail (p≈0.005). This is a nice scalar check but extremely limited in scope.

What is *not* demonstrated, despite being central to the claimed “unified workflow”:

- That ρ\_s practically identifies meaningful training points in any real attribution task (bias, privacy, hallucinations). No experiments: no dataset debugging, no removal/relabelling and re-training to see if behavior changes as predicted.
- That the ω-based “steer vs. retrain” decision rule is effective. There is no systematic study showing: when ω is high, steering works well and influence updates add little; when ω is low, steering systematically fails in ways that weight edits fix. Without that, the “no-free-lunch” theory remains a geometric sanity check rather than a validated engineering diagnostic.
- That the methods “scale to billion-parameter models.” All shown models (GPT-2 Medium, ResNet-50) are modest by current standards. The paper claims computational primitives are cheap (two JVPs, small pseudoinverse), but does not report runtimes, memory footprints, or any results on genuinely large LMs (e.g., ≥13B, let alone 70B) where Jacobian computations, Hessian inverses, and pseudoinverses at intermediate layers can be nontrivial.
- Any **robustness** assessment: how sensitive is IAS to Hessian approximations, damping φ, or sub-sampling when estimating influence? This matters particularly given known fragility of influence functions in deep nets.

Given these gaps, the paper does not substantiate the ambitious framing (“single, efficient workflow for controllability and data provenance,” “practical diagnostic,” “scale to billion-parameter models”). The theory may be sound locally, but the empirical section is not strong enough to demonstrate broad practical viability or to justify the applied claims.

### 4. Generalization bound under low-rank IAS is largely boilerplate and not clearly connected to real steering practice  
**Type: Methodological gap (borderline evidential)**  
**Where:** Section 6, Theorem 6.1 and follow-up text.

The paper derives a Rademacher complexity bound using results from Pinto et al. (2024), getting an additional term O(α L √(2k/(d n))) for a rank-k IAS modification at a layer of width d. This is likely mathematically correct as far as it goes, but:

- It essentially restates a generic low-rank-perturbation result; there is no argument that this bound is specifically tight or informative for the way steering is done in the paper (e.g., magnitudes of α used in detox experiments, ranks actually employed).
- There is no empirical connection: no experiments varying rank k and α to show that generalization or test loss tracks the bound or that “benign” complexity blow-up matters in practice.
- Critically, steering in the paper is not always implemented as an explicit low-rank *weight* correction UV; the formalism is in activation space. The translation to a rank-k weight-layer change is indicated but not fleshed out in the text we see; it is not obvious that real steering baselines they compare against are within that low-rank class.

This section reads as an add-on to tick a “generalization” box rather than a core contribution that influences the paper’s main claims. It does not materially support the promised “generalization bounds for low-rank steering interventions” in a way that changes how IAS would be used.
